JL JL Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this honourable House to attend His Majesty, immediately in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend His Majesty.

And being returned j

Outlawry . A Bill for the more effectual preventing Clandestine Bill. Outlawries, was read the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

The King’s Mr. Speaker reported, that the House had attended reported. Majesty in the House of Peers; where His Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the

Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which Mr. Speaker said lie had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The high Price of Wheat, and the defective Produce of that Grain last Harvest, together with the extraordinary Demands for the same from foreign Parts, have principally determined Me to call you thus early together, that I might have the Sense of Parliament, as soon as conveniently might be, on a Matter so important, and particularly affecting the poorer Sort of My Subjects.

The Urgency of the Necessity called upon Me, in the mean Time, to exert My Royal Authority for the Preservation of the Public Safety, against a.growing Calamity, which could not admit of Delay. I have therefore, by and with the Advice of My Privy Council, laid an Embargo on Wheat and Wheat-flour goingout of the Kingdom, until the Advice of Parliament could be taken thereupon.

If further Provisions of Law be requisite or expedient with regard to the Dearness of Com, so necessary to the Sustenance of the poorer Sort, they cannot escape the Wisdom of Parliament, to which I recommend the due Consideration thereof.

At the same Time I mull with Concern take Notice, that notwithstanding My Cares, for My People, a Spirit Vjjl. 31.

of the most daring Insurrection has in divers Parts broke forth in Violences of the most criminal Nature.

Necessary Orders have been given for bringing such dangerous Offenders to condign Punishment, and speedy Justice; nor shall Vigilance and Vigour on My Part be wanting, to restore Obedience and Rev©, rence to Law and Government.

I have the Satisfaction to inform you, that, lince I last met you, I have concluded a Treaty of Commerce with My good Sifter the Empress of Russia, whereby that cohsiderable Branch of Trade is fixed on a just and satisfactory Footing.

It is with Pleasure that I also acquaint you, that the Marriage between My good Brother the King of Denmark and My Sifter the Princess Caroline Mathilda has been felemnized, and the natural Alliance between the Two Crowns happily strengthened by an additional Tye of so agreeable a Nature.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered the proper Ellimates for the current Service of the Year to be laid before you.

Such Supplies as you may grant shall be duly applied with the utmost Fidelity, and strictest Regard to the Objects for which they are granted.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The general Posture of Affairs in Europe affords no Occasion to lay any Thing new before you upon that Head. My purposes are constant and fixt to maintain, on My Part, the Public Tranquillity inviolate; and to support the Dignity of My Crown, and the Rights of My Subjects. Ibe Justice and Wisdom of the other great Powers of Europe leave no room to apprehend any Intentions of a contrary Nature.

A Petition of the Mayor, Merchants, and principal Inhabitants of the Borough of King's Lynn, in the County of Norfolk, was presented to the House and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners being thoroughly convinced of the universal Scarcity of Wheat and Rye in this Kingdom, as well by the extravagant Prices they now bear, even in that County, so remarkable for its Growth and Plenty, as by their general Correspondence with other Corn Counties, do humbly apprehend, That, at this Juncture, an Act for the Importation of said Grain, Duty free, is not.only expedient, but highly necessary, for the Reduction of the present high Prices: And therefore praying. That a Bill may forthwith pass into a Law, for the above Purpose; or to give such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for allowing the Importation of Wheat and Wheat-flour, from any Part of Europe, into this Kingdom, for a Time to be limited, free of Duty, is committed.

W ere severally presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of the 1 louse, that a Bill is. depend* ing, for prohibiting the making of Starch from Wheat or Wheat-flour; and aftedging. That the Quantity of Wheat and Wheat-flour,.goufumed in making of Starch, is small apd inconliderable, and the Quality in general of an inferior Sort, unfit for the making of Bread; that the principal Confuniption of Starch aril’es from the L'fe necessarily made thereof in the several Trades and Manufactures carried on by the respective Petitioners, and without which the same could not be carried on; and that no substitute hath hitherto been discovered for the making of Starch, in the Head of Wheat or Wheat-flour, but is equally hurtful to the Poor and the Public; and that the whole Quantity of Wheat consumed in making Starch, if converted into Bread, (much the greater Part whereof from its Quality, it is impossible so to convert) would not, as will appear from Calculation, afford more than One Pound Bread, One Day in a Year, to One Half Part of the Nation: And therefore praying the House to take into Consideration the several Allegations in their Petitions; and that, if it shall seem meet, the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or their Counsel in Support thereof.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for making more effectual an Act, passed in the Third Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for vesting Part of the settled Estates of Samuel Dash-wood, Esquire, in Trustees, for raising Money to pay Debts and Incumbrances, and for providing an Equivalent or Compensation for the fame, to the Issue inheritable under his Marriage Settlement; to which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

Colne River A Petition of several Noblemen, and the humble Pe-M to tition of several Gentlemen, whose Names are thereunto

anai-0"6 subscribed, in Behalf of themselves and others, was pre- fented to the House and read; Setting forth, That many of the Inhabitants of the City and Liberty of Westminster,of Saint Mary le Bone, and of the Parishes adjacent, are badly supplied with Water; and that the , Petitioners, from accurate Surveys made, find that a

proper Supply of Water may be had from a Branch of the River Colne, near the Colour Mill, about Half a Mile below Uxbridge, which may be brought by a Canal, to be made for that Purpose, to a Place near William's Farm House, in the Parish of Saint Mary le Bone aforesaid; and, as the making such Canal navigable has been thought to be of great Utility to the l\iblic, the Petitioners are willing to undertake the fame; and that Three Mills will be destroyed by means of this Undertaking, the Loss whereof may be supplied by others to be erected on a Stream near adjoining, called the High Stream, where there is Waste Land of little Value, which the Petitioners are willing to purchase, and thereon to erect such Mills, or to make Satisfaction for the fame, as shall be thought proper; and that the Petitioners have heard that some Doubts have arisen whether the taking the Water from the River Colne aforesaid may not in some small Degree injure the Navigation of the River Thames, at certain Shallow

Places, near Cherlfey, Shepperton, and; the

Petitioners arc not apprehensive that any such Injury can arise; however, as the Navigation at those Places is confelfedly inconvenient, the Petitioners, to remedy such Inconvenience, are willing, and propole (on such Terms as shall be thought proper to be settled by Parliament) to make proper navigable Cuts, and erect Locks through the Land adjoining to tliofc Places, for the Purposes of avoiding the said Shallow's, and to support such Cuts and Locks in a proper Manner; whereby not only every Objection w'ill be wholly obviated, but the Navigation of the River Thames will be greatly improved; and that the Petitioners have a Proposal depending for an Agreement with the Governor and Company of CheljiaWater Works, for uniting the Petition-

ers Undertaking to bring the Water from the Colne aforesaid, with the said*Company, and making them One United Company, with a joint Stock; and that the Advantages resulting to the Public from the Execution of those Designs are, as the Petitioners conceive, great and obvious; but the same cannot be carried into Exe-tion without the Aid of an Act of Parliament: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the several Purposes aforesaid, w’ith such Powers, and under such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem proper.

Officers

Widows*.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That, in the Time of War, a Widow* of a Captain usually received per Annum the Sum of Forty-Five Pounds, the Widow of a Lieutenant and Matter Thirty Pounds, the Widow of a Boatlwain, Gunner, Carpenter, Purler, Surgeon, and feeonil Master, Twenty Pounds, which Sums, in the printed Papers

7 Geo. III. 29* Jc

pepg published by the Admiralty, and delivered to the Petitioners at the Time of Payment, are called the full Peulions established by his late Majesty: but, for these Three Years, their Pensions hat e annually decreased, and are now so greatly diminilhcd, that many are rc-dueed to infupcrable and aliuoit insupportable Dillrefs;

s and, without the kind Intcrpolitiou and Relief of the

'c, House, their present very calamitous Situation is likely

to be rendered Hill more intolerable, by the excessive Dearness of Provisions, and the Crueljy of merciless Creditors, many of the unhappy Petitioners being now under continual Fears and Apprehcnlions of a Gaol, and iome confined in Prison for small Debts, not being able to raise any Money on the Credit of their nominal Pensions, being neither certain of the Sum to be received, nor the Time of Payment; and that the poor diltrelfed Petitioners cannot help thinking their same peculiarly singular and unfortunate.; and that the Peace, which was so defrrable to all, not only for the Security of Tfade, but on account of the immense Expence, and the Horrors and Devastations of War, has been alone fatal to them; every Reduction in the Navy, and the Savings thereby made to the Public, being a Reduction of the Pensions of the poor unhappy unfortunate Widow’s of those Men who put His Majesty’s Enemies into His Hands, secured His Subjects from dreaded and threatened Invasions, protected their Lives and Fortunes, and procured their Security and Happiness, at the Hazard and Expence of their own; Men, to whom (as some Plea in Favour of the Petitioners) they hope they may be permitted to say, this Nation is partly indebted for Victories, Conquests and Triumphs, which raised the Reputation of the British Arms to the iiigheli Pitch of Glory, and secured immense Acquilitions to the Crown of Great , at the Close

of a long, bloody, and expensive War: The unhappy Petitioners therefore most humbly hope. That the dip-x tinguished Services rendered to the Public by their brave but unfortunate Hidbands, w ill recommend them and their helpless Orphans to the Notice of Parliament; and they flatter themselves, that, as the Land Officers Widows are regularly paid every Four Months by a Parliamentary Settlement, the House will so far concur in -his late Majesty’s most humane and Royal Intention; of focusing a Settlement for the Widpws of Naval Officers, that, by the Authority of Parliament, their Pensions may />e fixed and regularly paid, which many of their Iluffiands have dearly purchased with the Price of their Blood.

Woollen Cloth, of which the said Company, for a long Term of Years, did not -export less than 16,000 Pieces, and very considerable Quantities of Tin, Lead, and other Goods; and the chief Imports have been raw Materials for our Manufactures, such as Silk, Mohair, Yarn; Cotton, and Goat’s Wool; and also Fruit, Drugs, and many other Commodities; and that the saidTrade,to and from once

And that the Wharfs between Paul’s Wharf, in the City of London, and Milford Lane, in the county of ,

by their different Encroachments, not only form an irregular and disagreeable Outline, but afford the Owners of some an undue Preference and Advantage over others, at the same Time that the reflected Set of the Tides, both of Ebb and Flood, throws the Force of the Stream upon the Surrey Shore, oppositeto

and of consequence slackens the Current on the London Side; which, together with the large Sewers that empty themselves in the Neighbourhood, occasions a conllant Accumulation of Sand, Mud, and Rubbish, and thereby not only destroys great Part of the Navigation, at Low Water, but renders the Wharfs inaccessible, by the loaded Craft, even at High Water, unless at Spring Tides; that the Petitioners are advised all these Inconveniences might be removed, if the North Side of the River was embanked, so as to range in a Line with the North Entrance of the said intended Bridge, the North Butment of which is so constructed, as that it may, at the Expence of Labour only, be made to coincide therewith, and the Expence of such Embankment is estimated at the Sum of £. 7,500. And that the Royal Exchange, originally erected by Sir Thomas,

under the Aulpices of Queen Elizabeth, and rebuilt soon after the Fire of London in 1666, is so much de-caj7ed as to threaten its total Demolition, unless speedily and effectually repaired; and that the said ne-celfury Repairs are estimated at the Sum of £. 10,000, a Sum which the present State of the Revenues appropriated thereto can by no Means afford. And that the Goal o i Nnegate,which is not only the County Gaol

of Middlesex, as well as London, but the general Prison for State Prisoners, and Smugglers from all Parts of the Kingdom, is so final] and ill contrived, that it is impossible to accommodate the unhappy Persons confined there, with a suficient Supply of fresh Air and W ater, the Debtors Side not enjoying even the common Benefit of Light in any Hour of the Day, or at any Season of the Year; from which Circumstances the said Gaol is in general unhealthy, and often visited with a malignant Fever, called the Goal Distemper, the fatal Effects of which have sometimes extended beyond the Prison Walls; besides which, the said Goal is so old and ruinous, as to be incapable of Improvement, or any tolerable Repair; and that the rebuilding the said Goal in a more airy and commodious Manner is estimated at the Sum of £.50,000; Aud that the said several Sums 16

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Philip Smith and Robert Holyday said, That the Road from Stonehouse to Plymouth is over the Ferry at Stunelioiife Creek,mid is the nearest Way from Plymouth to the Dock.

That the Avenues to and from the said Ferry are very narrow and incommodious, so that the Ferry, can only be made use of by Pafi’engers on Foot.

That if a safe and commodious Bridge was built over the said Creek, and convenient Avenues opened from the same to the Town of Plymouth and Plymouth Dock, it would make a fhnrter and more easy Communication between the said Town and Dock. And they added,

That the Owners of the present Ferry are deiirous to build such a Bridge, and to open such Communication in case they shall be impowered so to do.

Mr. Couse was then directed to apply to Thomas Worjley, Esquire, Surveyor General, and the rest of the Commissioners of the Board of Works, that Plans of proper Accommodations might be prepared, together with an Estimate of the Expence, exclusive of the Purchase of the Premises; and accordingly he produced Plans, which are hereunto annexed, marked B, which shews the Buildings as they are at present; and the two Plans C and D, fixed thereon, contain a Delign for a Stair-Cafe, with Rooms and Passages for the accommodating of this House; and are made conformable to the Building now carrying on for the Office of Ordnance, in Saint Margaret's Street, and which is Part of the general Design, for new Offices for Records, &c. and which hereafter will remain, for Accommodations to this House, whenever the same shall be re-built; The upper Story will ferveat present for the Reception of Papers from the Augmentation Office, Sic.which cannot be pulled down till proper Places are built to receive them; and which may then be carried back to the Placesto bebuiltfor that Purpose. He is of Opinion that the Expence of this Plan, exclusive of the Purchase, will be about £. 4,150.

He also, by Order of your Committee, produced the Plans E and F, which thovvs how a Stair-Cafe and other Rooms might be built on the West Side of the Court of Requests; but apprehended that would not be so well included in the general Delign before mentioned; and that the Expence, exclusive of the Purchase, will be about £.2,300.

Whereupon the Committee came to the following Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That if the Delign for the Building, marked C and D, upon the Plan marked B, was carried into Execution, proper and sufficient Accommodations would be made for the Members, in their Railage to and from this House.

N. B. The Plans, marked B, C, D, E, and F, are preferred with the Report.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, Mr. William Pet, Harness-maker, at Whitechapel, being examined, said. That his Father lately bought Two Chaldrons of Coals, which, upon being re-measured, appeared to want Four Bushels of Measure.

Mr. Samuel Elkin, Weaver at Shoreditch, informed your Committee, that he lately bought Ten Chaldron of Coals, which were found to be Twenty-one Bushels deficient in Measure.

Mr. Goddard Williams, Sadler in Great Queen Street, being examined, said. That about Three Years ago, he bought Coals, in the City of London, which were Three Buihels and One Peck, in a Chaldron, short of Measure.

Mr. Henry Hall, Broker in Moor Fields, being examined, said, That in Ai/gujl -1765 he bought Five Chaldron of Coals, which wanted Thirty-one Bushels of Measure.

To prove the Allegations of the second-mentioned Petition,

Mr. Joseph Harrison, Mr. Coltman, and Mr.

John Waller, Dealers in Coals, being severally examined, said. That frequent Frauds are committed in the admeasuring of Coals; and that the Dealers in Coals are frequently harassed with frivolous and groundless Complaints and Prosecutions, on account of the Measure of Coals sold by them, by People who have lately set themselves up as Informers, and frequently bring Prosecutions where neither the Coal-dealer or his Servants have been in any Fault: And that it would be a great Security, both to the Dealers in Coals and the Consumers, if an Office w as established, and proper Persons appointed to inspect the Admeasurement of Coals within the City of London and Liberties thereof, and between the Tower of London and Limehoitfe-hole.

A Petition of the Royal Boroughs of Scotland, met Whal* at Edinburgh the 30th Day of January 1767, was pre- Fishery. fented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Bounty of Forty Shillings per Ton, granted by Parliament on all Ships employed in catching Whales, in the 1 Greenland Seas, expires at the End of this present Session of Parliament; and that the said Branch of Commerce, the Petitioners think, is an Object of National Importance; and the Shortness of the Time granted for the Continuance of the Bounty, by the lall Act of Parliament, it is believed, has checked the Increase of that Fishery; and it is greatly to be feared, if the Bounty is not renewed, that that valuable Branch of Trade will be entirely at a (land: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and to do in it as to them shall seem meet.

the Monies received and disbursed in pursuance of the said Act, by which it appeared that all the Money received had been expended, and that there is now owing on the Credit of the said Act the Sum 503. 1 5

And he informed your Committee, that the Produce of the Duty, during the subsisting Term in the said Act, will not be sufficient to discharge the said Debt, and finish the intended Plan of Improvements, so as to render the said Harbour safe and commodious.

Mr. Richard Grindley,further said, That Two Quays

have been built, but the Heads still want inclosing, and several Repairs are also wanting.

That there are many Coal-works and Salt-W'orks carried on near the said Town; and that the Engines made use of for carrying on these Works have entirely drained every Spring Well in the Town, and it is necessary to bring a fresh Supply of wholesome Water, at a great Expence, there being none at present within a less Distance than Half aMile,except such ascomes from the Coal Ix’vel, which is very bad.

That the Streets in the said Town are in very bad Repair, and the Avenues to it stand in great Need of being opened, in order to render the said Town more commodious; and that there is no Road to the said Town from the Wefnvard.

That great Disorders happen in the Harbour, and great Damage is frequently done to the Quays and Shipping, for want of Power to oblige Ships to remove from the Loading and Discharging-Births, when others ought to come in That the Trustees have appointed a Harbour Mailer for the better regulating the Shipping, but as he is not in vetted with proper Powers, his Appointment has had little Effect

Tl»at the Trade of the said Town is, of late Years, greatly increased; but there is not any Fund for the Execution of any Work for public Utility.

That when the said Act passed, it was apprehended that the whole Parish of Borrowstounness was liable to pay the aforesaid Duty; but, by a Determination of the Court of Session, it is now confined to the Town.

Mr. Hamilton, being again examined, said, That the Works necessary to be done, in and about the said Town, would amount to £. 4,900, viz. 3,500 for repairing the Harbour; £.800 for supplying Water; and £.600 for widening and repairing the Streets.

to Nottingham Trent Bridge, with other Roads therein mentioned; in w;hich said Bill, ns the Petitioners are informed, is intended to be inserted a Clause to enforce an Annual Account, and Payment of One Moiety of the Tolls collecded,or to be collected, upon the Whole of the said Road, to the Treasurer for the Eastern Part thereof; which, if passed into a Law, will be very detrimental to the Petitioners, the said Mortgagees, who, with others, have advanced £. 4,750 towards the Repair of the said Road; and that it was, by the said former Act, declared, that the Residue of the Tolls arising, and Monies to be borrowed (certain Payments thereout being first deducted) in or in respect of the said Road should be applied in equal Moieties, in repairing and widening such Parts thereof as lead from Grantham to the Top of Elton Hill, and from the Top of Elton Hill to Nottingham Trent Bridge; which Clause, th- Petitioners apprehend, w'as inserted upon a Pcefumption that the Expence of keeping in Repair each Division would be nearly equal; but it is demonstrable that the Weliern Division is, and ever will remain,much more expensive than the Ealiern; the Tolls arising w'ilhin the Western Division amounting, communibus Annis, to Five Parts in Six of the Whole, besides the many Compositions to which the Western Division is liable; and that the said former Act was passed in 1759; from which Time to the 31st of May 1763, before the capital Sum borrowed was expended, the Treasurer for the Western Division regularly paid a Moiety of the clear Tolls to the Treasurer of the Eastern: but, in the Year 1764, several Parts of the Road were in a very ruinous Condition, particularly in Whatlon Field,which lies in the Center thereof, and Part of the Western Division was totally impassable with any degree of Safety, even for a Angle Horse, whereby the Communication betw'een Grantham and Nottingham was in a great measure stopt, and the Country in general highly dissatisfied on that Account; the acting Trustees residing in the Western Division, as.well-.-to open ihe Communication (without which the Tolls must necessarily have been greatly reduced, the Subscribers in general thereby injured, and the Road rendered, comparatively useless)thought proper to expend the then current Tolls of Gamfion and Thorough Bridge Gates, and to borrow 150 to make that Part of the Road pallable; that this extraordinary Expence of the Western Division

fiij/hway; Mr.' Kynaston reported from the Committee, who* were appointed to revise and consider of the general ws* Laws, relating to the Public Highways and Turnpike Roads in that Part of Great Britain called England; and to report their Opinion to the House thereupon, and also concerning any Alterations, Amendments, or Repeal, of the fame, which they may think necessary, towards the making of more effectual Provisions for amending and preserving the said Highways and Roads; that the Committee had revised and considered the said Laws accordingly; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the general Laws relating to the Highways and Turnpike Roads are so numerous and complicated, that, by reason of the Difficulty of ascertaining and reconciling their Meaning, they frequently remain unexecuted.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That several Provisions of the said Laws are ineffectual for the Purposes intended.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no sufficient and effectual Method is prescribed by the present Laws, for t^e Appointment ef able and skilful Persons to actas Surveyors of the Highways.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Statute Labour, directed by the said Laws, is unequally burthensome, and frequently evaded, or at lealt ineffectually performed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That. the present Methods of regulating the Weight of Carriages, and the Number of Ilorfes, are, in feme Cafes, attended with Inconveniences.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, 'That if all the general Laws respecting the Highways and Turnpike Roads were to be reduced into One or more Act or Acts, with proper Alterations and Amendments, the good Purposes thereby intended might be moreNeffectually carried, into Execution.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

American The Lord Clare, from the Commissioners for Trade Trade, and Plantations, acquainted the House, that His Majesty had commanded them to inform the House, that they had received, inclosed in a Letter from Sir Henry Moore, Baronet, His Majesty’s Governor of New York, a Petition of the Merchants in the City of New York, in the Colony of New Yoi'k, in America, addressed to the House of Commons, which, the Governor fays, he trans-14

mitted to the Commissioilersef Trade and Plantations, at the ltequest of a Committee of Merchants of New , York.

And the Lord Clare opened to the House the Con- . tents of the said Petition.

Ordered, That the said Petition be brought up.

Then the said Petition was brought up, arid read; Setting forth. That the Commerce of the North American Colonies is so severely clogged and reliriCled by the Statutes of the Fourth and Sixth of His present Majesty, as to afford a melancholy Presage of its Destruction, the fatal Effects of which, though first felt there, must finally be transferred to Great Britain, and center with her Merchants and Manufacturers; that anEvil so extensive could not fail of alarming the Petitioners, whose Situation exposes them to the first Impression of this Calamity; and that they therefore think it their Duty to implore the House to resume the Consideration of the Plantation Trade, for effectual Redress; and representing, that it is the Angular Disadvantage of the Northern British Colonies, that, while they stand in need of vast Quantities of the Manufactures of Great Britain, the Count ry is productive of very little which affords a direct Remittance thither in Payment; and that from Necessity therefore, the Inhabitants have been driven to seek a Market for their Produce, where it could be vended, and, by aCourse of Traffick, to acquire either Money or such Merchandize as would answer the Purpose of a Remittance, and enable them to sustain their Credit with the Mother Country; that the Prodigious Balance arising in her Favour is a FaCfctoo well known to the Merchants of Great Britain trading to those Parts, to need any Elucidatiod; but, as the Nature of the Petitioners Commerce, when free from the late Restraints, ought to be understood, they beg Leave to observe, that their Produce then feat to our own and the foreign Islands, was chiefly bartered for Sugar, Rum, Molasses, Cotton, and Indigo; that the Sugar, Cotton, and Indigo,served as Remittance to Great Britain; but the Rum and Molasses constituted essential Branches of the Petitioners Commerce, and enabled them to barter with our own Colonies for Fish and Rice, and by that Means to pursue a valuable Trade with Spain, Portugal, and Italy, where they chiefly obtained Money or Bills of Exchange in Return; and likewise qualified them for Adventures to Africa, where they had the Advantage of putting off great Quantities of British Mmu-t factures, and of receiving in Exchange, Gold, Ivory, and Slaves, which last, disposed of in the West India Islands, commanded Money or Bills; Rum was indispensable in their Indian Trade; and, with British Manufactures, procured Furs and Skins, which served for considerable Returns to Great Britain, and increased the Revenue thereof; that the Trade to the Bay of Honduras was also very material to their Commerce, being managed with small Cargoes of Provisions, Rum, and British Manufactures, which, while they were at Liberty to fend foreign Logwood to the different Ports in 23wr0/;e,fumished them with another valuable Branch of Remittance; that, from this View, it is evident, that Sugar, Rum, Molasses, and Logwood, with Cotton and Indigo, are the Efleiw tials of their Return Cargoes, and the chief Sources from which, in a Course of Trade, they have extended their Usefulness to, and maintained their Credit with, Great Britain; that, considering the prodigious Consumptioji of West India Produce in Great Britain, Ireland, and the Continental Colonies, the rapid Increase of thqfe Colonies, their Inhabitants already exceeding Two Millions, the vast Accession of Subjects by the late Conquests, be-(ides the innumerable Tribes of Indians in the extensive Countries annexed to the BritJh Crown, the utter Incapacity of our own Islands to supply so great a Demand, will, the Petitioners presume, be out of all Question; on the other Hand, the Lumber produced from clearing this immense Territory, and Provision extracted from a fertile Soil, which most of the Inhabitants are employed in cultivating, must raise a Supply for Exportation, with which the Confuinption of our own Islands can bear no

fort


7 Geo. Ill* i6°

fort of Proportion; that it seems therefore consistent with found Policy to indulge those Colonies in a free and unrestrained Exportation of all the Lumber and Produce they raise and can spare, and an ample Importation of Sugar, Rum, and Molasses, to supply the various Branches of their Trade, to which they appear so necessary; that, without the one, the clearing of new Lands, which is extremely laborious and expensive, will be discouraged; and Provisions, for Want of vent, become of little Profit to the Farmer; without the other, the Petitioners mult be plunged into a total Incapacity of making good their Payments for British Debts; their Credit multiink, and their Imports from Great Britain gradually diminish, till they are contrasted to the narrow Compass of Remittances, barely in Articles of their own Produce; and that, how little soever their Interest of Commerce could be promoted, the Colonies thus checked, mult, from inevitable Neceljity betake themselves to Manufactures of their own, which will be attended with Consequences very detrimental to those of Great Britain-, and that the Petitioners, having thus represented the Nature of their Commerce, humbly beg Leave to point out the several Grievances which it labours under, from the Regulations prescribed by the Tw o before-mentioned Acts; and which, if not remedied, they conceive mufti have a direct Tendency to prevent the Cultivation, and ruin the Trade, of the Colonies, and prove highly pernicious to both the Landed and Trading Interest of Great Britain; that the heavy Embarrassments^ which attend the Article of Sugar, is a capital Subject of Complaint; and, besides the absolute Necessity of a great Importation to sustain their Trade, it is a well known Truth, that it often happens, at the foreign Islands with which they have Intercourse, that a sufficient Return Cargo, independent bfSugar, cannot be procured, which alone mult render Trade precarious and discouraging; but the high Duty of Five Shillings Sterling a Hundred is proved, by Experience, to be excessive, and has induced the fair Trader to decline that Branch of Business, while it presents an irresistable Incentive to Smuggling, to People less fcru-pulous; that it answers not the Purposes of the Government, or of the Nation, lince it cannot be duly collected, and, if it could, would have a necessary Tendency to contract Remittances for British Debts, w hile, at the same Time, it is most mischievous to the Colonies, by cutting off One of the grand Springs of their Traffick; and, that the Pressure of this Duty is not aggravated, the Petitioners appeal to the Officers of the Customs of their Port, who are Witnesses of the Impradicability of coliefling it, and who must confess, that there have not wanted lnllances, where Merchants have been driven to the disagreeable Necessity of bringing their very Plate into the Custofn House to discharge it; and that the Petitioners therefore most humbly intreat, that a moderate Duty be laid on foreign Sugars, which, they are assured, would not only greatly conduce to the Prosperity of those Colonies, and their Utility to the Mother Country, but increase the Royal Revenue far beyond what ctfn be expected under the present Restraints; that the compelling Merchants to land and storo foreign Sugars in Great Britain, before they can be exported to other Parts of Europe, is another most expensive and dilatory Restriction, without being of any material Advantage to the Revenue of Great Britain -, for it effectually puts it out of the Petitioners Power to meet ForeignersatMar-ket upon an equal Footing, is a great and heavy Burthen inTimes of Peace, and Security, but in War will expose the Trader to such Peril and Hazard, as mull \Vholiy extinguish this useful Branch of Remittance; that British Plantation Sugar, exported from North America, should be declared French on being landed in England, the Petitioners conceive mayjuftiy be classed among the Number of Hardships inflicted by those Regulations; as in effect it deprives them of making a Remittance in that Article, by exposing them to the Payment of the foreign Dpty in Great Britain^ which appears the more Vol. 31.

159

severe, as their Fellow Subjects of the Islands are left at Liberty to export those Sugars for what they really are, and a Distinction is thus created in their Favour, which the Petitioners cannot but regard with Uneasiness; that foreign Rum, French excepted, is the next Article wrhich the Petitioners most humbly propose for Consideration, as the Importation thereof, on a moderate Duty, would add considerably to the Revenue, prevent Smuggling, promote the Petitioners Navigation, increase the vent of their own Produce with British Manufactures, and enable them to bring back the full Value of their Cargoes, more especially from the Danish Islands of Saint Thomas and Saint Croix, from whence they can now only receive half the Value in Sugar and Cotton, eonfequently Rum alone can be expected for the other half, those Islands affording nothing else for Returns, and having no Specie but of a base kind; that the Exportation of foreign Logwood to foreign Markets, has already been distinguished as . one of the principal Means, by which those Colonies have been enabled to sustain the Weight of their Debts for British Manufactures, and it is with the greatest Concern, the Petitioners observe it to be ranked by the late Ad among the enumerated Articles; and eonfequently made subject to the Delay, the Hazard, and Expence, of being landed in Great Britain; the low Price of Logwood, its Bulk, and the Duty with which it is now burthened, must totally destroy that valuable Branch of the Petitioners Commerce, and throw it into the Hands of Foreigners, unfettered with those heavy Embarrassments; that their Lumber and Pot-alh, even when shipped for Ireland, where they are so necessary, the latter parti-, cularly for the Progress of their Linen Manufacture, and Provisions themselves, though intended to relieve that Kingdom from a Famine, are subject to the same distreffing Impediments; nor is Flax-feed, on the timely Importation of which the very Existence of the Linen Manufacture of Irelandimmediately depends, exempted; although it is a Fad capable of the most satisfactory Proof, that, without the Delay now created, it has been with Difficulty transported from that Colony, to be there in proper Season for sowing; that what renders so injurious an Obstruction the more affecting ,is the Reflection, that, while it deprives the Petitioners of the Benefits arising from Flax-feed, Lumber, and Pot-aih, these Articles may all be imported into Ireland directly from the Baltic, where they are purchased from Foreigners, under the national Disadvantage of being paid for with Money- instead of Manufactures; and the Petitioners therefore humbly beg Leave to express their Hopes, that an Evil in so high a Degree per-, nicious to them, to the Staple of Ireland, and to the Trade and Manufactures of Great Britain, and which inTimes of War must fall on all with a redoubled Weight, will not fail of obtaining the Attention of the House, and an immediate and effectual Red refs; and that the Petitioners beg Leave further to represent, that the Wines from the Islands, in Exchange for Wheat, Flour, Fish, and Lumber, would considerably augment the important Article of Remittance, was the American Duty withdrawn, on Exportation to Great Britain; and that it is therefore humbly Submitted to the House, whether such an Expedient, calculated at once to attach them to Husbandry, by expanding the Consumption of American Produce, to encourage British Manufactures by enabling the Petitioners to make good their Payments, and to increase the Royal Revenue by an additional Import of Wines into Great Britain, will not be confident with the united Interests both of the Mother Country and her Colonies; and that the Petitioners conceive the North American Fishery to be an Object of the highest national Importance; that nothing is so essential fortho Support of Navigation, since by employing annually so great a Number of Shipping, it constitutes a respect* able Nursery for Seamen, and is so clearly advanta-, geous for Remittances, in Payment so^ British Manufee*

tures; that the Petitioners therefore humbly presume, that it will becheriflied by the House with every possible Mark of Indulgence and every Impediment be remov-. ed, which tends to check its Progress; that the enlarg-, ing the Jurisdiction of the Admiralty, is another Part of the Statute of the Fourth of His present Majesty, very grievous to the Trade and Navigation of the Colonies, and oppressive to the Subject; the Property of the Trader being open to the Invasion of every Informer, and the Means of Justice so remote as to be scarcely attainable; that the Petitioners beg Leave to express the warmest Sentiments of Gratitude, for the Advantages intended by Parliament, to America in general, in the opening Free Ports at the I Hands of Jamaica and Dominica; yet at the same Time, they cannot but lament, that it is their Unhappiness to be in no Condition to reap the Benefits which, it was imagined, would flow from so wife a Policy; that the collecting great Quantities of the Produce of Martinico, Gaudaloupe, ko. at thelfland of Dominica, will be the natural Consequence of opening that Port, and would prove of real Importance to those Colonies, were they at Liberty to bring them back, in return for their Lumber and Prci-visions; but, as they are now prohibited from taking anything, exceptMolaffes, and, it isjuftJy apprehended, there cannot be a sufficient Quantity of that Commodity to support any considerable Trade, the Petitioners think it evident that no substantial Advantage can be derived to them under such a Reliraint; that they are, at the same Time, at a Loss to discern the Principle on which the Prohibition is founded; for, since Sugar may be imported direct from the foreign Islands, it seems much more reasonable, to suffer it from a Free Port belonging to Great Britain-, that the Petitioners therefore humbly hope, that the House will think it equitable to adapt this Trade to their Circumstances, by granting them Liberty to import into the Colonies all West India Productions, in exchange for their Commodities; and that, upon the Whole, with the greatest Anxiety, the Petitioners find themselves obliged to inform the House, that although, at the last Session, the Necessity of relieving the Trade of those Colonies seems to have been universally admitted, and the tender Regard of Parliament for their Ilappiness highly distinguished, nevertheless, Experience has evinced, that the Commercial Regulations, then enacted, instead of remedying, have increased the heavy Burthen under which it already laboured; as, therefore, upon due Consideration, it will be manifest, that the Ability of those Colonies, to purchase the Manufactures of Great Britain, immediately depends upon, and is infeparately connected with, the Progress of their Commerce; and as that Ability only, by removing the Necelfity of Home Manufactures, will leave them at Liberty to pursue Agriculture, in which their trueInterest consists: Therefore praying the House lo take the several Matters, in the said Petition suggested, into their Consideration, and to grant such Relief therein as shall be thought confident with good Policy, and the mutual Interest of Great Britain and her Colonies.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. John Haggajion produced the original Account Book, signed by the said Trustees, whereby it appeared, that they have laid out in the Purchase of Lands and Tenements, and inbuilding and furnishing an Hospital, the Sum of £.4,010. 3 s. of d.; and that, by the said Expences, some great Losses, Taxes, and Law Charges, their Capital is now reduced to £. 1,804. 16 s. 4*/.

And Mr. Haggajion, being examined, said, That the said Sum is insufficient for carrying on so good a Design; and that several Noblemen and others have entered into a voluntary Subscription for making the said Hospital a General Hospital, and that the Sums following had been subscribed for that Purpose before Christmas lall, viz. £.478. 7s. for building, and £.235. gs. for general Use, besides an annual Subscription of £.472. 11s. od.

That the properest Place to erect this Toll Bar, would be at the Maypole in East Smithfield, act it would not assess any Persons but those that go to and from the Wharfs in St. Catherine's.

A Petition of several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, as well on behalf of themselves, as many others, Owners and Inhabitants of Houses, lying between the Mansion-house of the City of London, and the Opening, or Passage, where Moorgate flood, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of the House, that a Petition is presented by several Merchants, Traders, and others, for a Bill for opening a new Street, from the Mansion-house aforesaid, to communicate with the Prebendal Estate of Halliivell, and for other Purposes therein mentioned; and that these Petitioners apprehend, that should so much of the intended Scheme take place, as may tend to the Opening a new Street, from the Mansion-house to the Place where Moorgate formerly flood, and no farther, the same cannot be carried into Execution without pulling down and demolishing 300 Houses, and upwards, the Rents of which amount to^. 6,000. a Year at least; and that the Number of Houses to be built, in lieu thereof, will not amount to more than Fourscore, or thereabouts; and that several of the Petitioners, some of whom have purchased the Freehold and Inheritance of their respective Houses, and others, who are possessed of Leases for long Terms of Years, have laid out very large Sums of Money in repairing and improving their respective Estates, for the better enabling them to carij on and follow their respective Trades and Occupations; and that a great Number of Houses* situate in Cornhill, ThreadnecdLc Street, Bartholomew Lane, and other Places, near The Bank of England, have lately been pulled down for the better Accommodation of the Bank, by wrhich Means the Occupiers thereof have been very much difirefi'ed, for w ant of proper Habitations to carry

lJ

on their respective Trades, and Houses are thereby become extremely scarce, and greatly inhanced in the Rents; and should the proposed demolifliing Plan take place, the Petitioners apprehend, it will be wholly impossible for many of them to accommodate themselves at any Rate: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against such Parts of the Petition as affects them, and to grant them such other Relief in the Premises as to the I louse shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to w hom the Petition , of the several Merchants, Traders, and others, residing^ within or constantly resorting to, the City of London, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, is referred; and that these Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their said Petition, if they think fit.

Marchwivei A Petition of the several Inhabitants of the Market

to Town of Malpas, in the County of Chester, and of the

*Roadtn Inhabitants of the Parities of Malpas, Tilfion, Shock-lack, and of the several Townships of Ckobnondeley, Bichley, Larton, Hampton Edge, Duckington, Macefen, Broxton, Chorltdn, Overton, Cuddington, Oldcafile, Nezv-ton, Bradley, Stockton, Wichough, Agden, Wigland, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners perceive, by the Votes, that Leave is given to bring in a Bill for repairing and widening the Hoad from Marchwivei, in the County of Denbigh, through Bangor, Worthenbury, and Hanmer, in the County of Flint, to a House in the Possession of Mr. Thomas Jenks, in the Parish of Whitchurch, in the County of Salop; and that there is another "Road from Bangor, through Malpas, passing also through that of Whitchurch, to Dodington, which runs nearly parallel with the intended Road from Bangor, through the Parishes of Worthenbury and Hanmer, to Dodington afore-% said; and that from Bangor, to the Bullring in Whitchurch, which is about the Center of the said Town, there is by Measurement but the Difference, of Half a Mile in Length between the Two Roads; and that this Difference may be reduced to a Quarter of a Mile, by the Purchase of a little Ground, to widen a Bridle Way, leading from Worthenbury, and entering upon Threapwood, by a House now in the Holding of Richard Morgan; and that, although the Road from Bangor to Malpas cannot be effectually repaired, and kept in ' Repair, by the Laws now in being, yet the intended Road, through the Parishes of Worthenbury and Hammer, is in a far more founderous Condition, and runs through a Country not so well provided of good Materials; that there is a good Pavement through the Town, and Part of the Township of Malpas; and that from Grindley Brook, where the Road from Malpas ]o\ns the Turnpike Road from Chester, there are, to Mr. Thomas Jenks's House in Dodington, Two Miles more, well repaired, and kept in Repair, at the Expence of the said Turnpike, and of the Town of Whitchurch, so that it is apprehended the Road through Malpas may be effectually repaired at a much easier Expence than the intended Road through Worthenbury and Hanmer; and that, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the Inhabitants of Malpas, and of the several Parishes and Townships aforesaid, and all Persons travelling between Malpas and Wrexham, would be subject to the Payment of Toll, on the said Road at Bangor, and have no Benefit of the Repair of the Road from that Place to Malpas: And therefore praying. That the Road from Bangor through Malpas may be the Road to be repaired, (instead of the Road through Worthenbury and Hanmer, to Dodington) as being not only less expensive, but also of equal, if not greater Public Utility, or that Provision may be made In the said intended Bill, for repairing the said Road from Bangor to Malpas also, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall feetti meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Cohsideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Jfaac Milburn, a Surveyor, being examined^ said, That lie knows the Country from Emetlland to Great Driffield; that he had surveyed the Rivers, Streams, and Becks, between those Places and the Country adjoining thereto, and had taken Levels for making a Navigation: that he made and took the said Survey and Levels by the Direction of Mr. Conyers of Malton, in pursuance of a Meeting of the principal Gentlemen of the County held at Driffield for that Purpose.

Mr. John Grundy, Engineer, being examined, said,

That he had seen the Survey, Levels, and Plan, taken by Mr. Milburn; and that he had upon the Spot C01U7 pared them with the Country, and found them true, from whence he drew a Plan for a Navigation, which may be easily made and completed agreeable thereto; and laid the same before the Committee: That he had likewise surveyed the River or Stream, from Froding-ham Bridge to the River Hull, which is not at present; navigable at all Times, but is capable of being made so: That the Expence of making and completing the said Navigation, from Emertland to Driffield, and from Frodingham Bridge to the River Hull, will be about £.7,450. And from his Observation he is of Opinion, that such Navigation may be carried into the Middle of the Town of Driffield, for the additional Expence of£-35°-

That the proposed Navigation will be a Means of draining the adjoining I^ands that are now subject to be overflowed, as he has calculated the Cuts to be made so deep, that the Surface of the navigable W^ter will be Two Feet under the Surface of those Lands, and by which Means the navigable Canals will serve as a Mother Drain for the Country.

That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

A State of the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition is as followeth; viz.

The Agent for the Petitioners produced the Probate of the Will of the said Mary Daffy, and also of the said Ann A Bon; whereby it appeared that Mary Daffy gave all her Estates tq her Sifter Ann Acton, who afterwards devised the same to Mary Brereton, her Niece.

And by the Evidence of General GanJ'elL it further appeared, that in the Rebellion in 1745, his Royal Highness the late Duke of Cumberland ordered the Witness to join General Douglas, and to aflllt him in the King’s Affairs, and that the General directed him to officiate as Engineer: That the General ordered him to make Report of the necessary Disposition for the Defence of the City and Castle.

That upon examining the Works, the Witness found it necessary, for the more immediate Safety of the Castle, to pull down several Houses that were directly opposite the weakest Part of it, and close adjoining to the Ditch of the Castle; which Houses, belonging to the late Mrs. Daffy, were situate in a Manor or Lord-lliip independant of the City or Castle, though within the City Walls.

That Lord Cholme ndeley,who was then Governor and Constable of ChefierC,astle, left it to the Witness to act upon the Occasion as he thought proper; whereupon the Witness went to Mrs. Daffy, and acquainted her that her Houses must be pulled down, and found Mrs.

Daffy very ready to consent that they should be taken down; and at the same time Ihe expressed the greatest Desire of doing every thing in her Power to assist His Majesty’s Affairs, and left it to the Witness to do with her Efitate what he should think most proper; and she added, that ffie took it for granted Ihe should be indemnified for the Losses ihe should sustain, as soon as the Troubles should be over.

The Witness remembers he told her, ihe need not in the least doubt the Justice of Government,- to indeni nify her for any Losses Ihe should receive in the Support of Government.

That Mrs. Daffy feerped extremely well satisfied, and even encouraged the Men in pulling down her Houses; that they were pulled down, and the Materials, such as Lead, Timber, fif c.were carried into the Castle. to be made use of for his Majesty’s Service, or returned to her: And the Witness added, that he particularly remembers a very fine Orchard was at the same Time destroyed, then in seeming Perfection, which, though not mentioned, he knows was Mrs. Daffy's Property.

That soon afterwards he went to and at his

Return which was about Two Years afterwards. Governor Popple acquainted him, that the Family of the Daffy's were applying to Government, in Order to obtain Satisfaction for the Damages they had sustained, for several Houses having been pulled down for the Security of the Castle of Chester in the late Rebellion, and which had not been included either in the Estimate made by Lord Cholmondeley of Damages sustained relative to the Defence of the Castle, or by the Magistrates of the

Town,

Town, as in fad not annexed to the Government of either, though situate between them.

The Governor then shewed the Witness an Estimaie of Damages sustained by Mrs. Daffy, attested by Two Surveyors on Oath, made before Mr. Salsbury and Mr.

Williams both of which Magistrates were intimately known to him the said Witness, amounting to between 6 and £.700 and the Witness then made this Observation to Governor Popple, " That he was extremely glad " to fee the Estimate was not greater, for that he thought " the Damage done upon that Spot mull have been " much more," and that he then alked if the Materials were included in this Estimate, and the Governor an-fvvered, he could not tell; that the Witness then said, as he could venture to declare upon his Oath, that the material Articles contained in that Estimate were true, there was all the Reason in the World to suppose the trilling Parts of it were also true; and that he thought there could be no Objection made by any one to affixing such an Attestation to the Estimate; and therefore the Witness accordingly did it.

That about a Year and an half aftenvards, the Witness met the late Mr. Salsbury, who told him, that the then Application to the Treasury had mifearried, through the Mismanagement of the Gentlemen who had undertaken to solicit the Affair.

That Dr. Suunton no sooner became possessed of the Eliate in Right of his Wife, but he frequently, and in the most earned and most pressing Manner, applied to the Witness to give him a fresh Attestation agreeable to the Purport of the First, which was millaid in the Treasury; but the Witness said, he was unwilling to give a Second Attestation, for fear there might be any Difference in them; but concluded with saying, that "he should think it his Duty, as an honest Man, to give Evidence to the Truth, whenever he should be called upon, but could not presume to make himself an officious Evidence, as it might give Offence.

That upon every Change in the Treasury the Do6tor has applied to the Witness, and he has always given him the same Answer.

And it further appeared to your Committee, that the principal Money Hated to the said Estimate, and the Interest thereupon at 5 Pounds per Centum per Annum, from the beginning of September 1745 to the present Time, amounts to the Sum of 1,435, or thereabouts.

Then Mr. Leake, a Clerk in the Treasury, produced a Copy of his Majesty’s Warrant, dated the ift of March 1747, directing Compensation to be made to the City of'Chester, and to several of the Inhabitants thereof, for the Losses sustained by them in the late Rebellion; and it docs not appear to your Committee, that the Amount of the Losses sustained by the said Mary Daffy are included in the said Warrant.

In Support of the Allegations of the First, Second, Third, and Fifth-mentioned Petitions, the Agent called Mr. John Miav; who said, that, if the Navigation was extended as high as to Ripon, it would be of great Benefit to the Inhabitants of Ripon and Boroughbridge, and also of the several Towns and Places near the said River, as it will reduce the Price of Carriage of Goods, and furnish Manure for the Lands near the lliver: That the Price of Carriage from York to Ripon is now Ten Shillings a Ton, and, when this Navigation is Completed, it will be reduced Three or Four Shilling:; a Ton: That Persons at Boroughbridge are obliged to fend their Goods by Land, as the Navigation of the River between Boroughbridge and Linton, is frequently obstructed by the Shallows in that Part of the lliver; but below Linton there is a Navigation at all 'Limes of the Year.

And being asked the Reason why the Price of Carriage of Goods between York and is higher than between York and Hu he laid that the Banks

of this Navigation are farmed by Two Persons only, who can prevent others from landing their Goods upon these Banks; and this, lie thinks, is the Reason of the Difference in the Price.

And being alked if there might not be other Banks made on the River for landing of Goods? he said there might below Linton, but they would be no Advantage

to Persons at Boroughbridge and Ripon. And being alked whether Persons have a Right to hale on the Banks of this River? he said, he thought they had, aa high as Boroughbridge.

Then, to shew that the River is capable of being made navigable, John S'meaton, Esquire, laid, that he had surveyed the River from Linton up to Ripon; that below Boroughbridge the Navigation does tolerably well, when the River is full of Water; yet, from the Number of Shoals {no less than Nine in Eight Miles, and all below the Mouth of the Swale but One) and from the Quantity of Fall in the River between Milby and Lifiton, which is Nine Feet, it appears that in dry Seasons those Shoals mull be very shallow: That in September last, when he founded that Part of the River, he found in several Places not above Two Feet Three Inches Water, altho’ the River at that Time was said to be in a good State for the Season of the Year; and that there mull certainly be a very imperfect Navigation in all dry Seasons. To confirm which,

Mr. Thomas Homer was called, who said, that in Augt/ft last, in different Places in the said River, there . was only from Twelve to Fourteen Inches Depth of Water. And,

would be raised so high as to make a complete Navigation to Milby at all Times of the Year: That above Milby he would make a Cut on the Side of the River, in the Manner laid down in a Plan which lie produced and explained to your Committee.

Then, to prove the Allegations in the Fourth-mentioned Petition, the Agent called,

Mr. Smeaton; who said he had taken a Level of the River Swale, from the Mouth thereof up to Helper by, and that the Fall is about Nine Feet; and that he had not the least Doubt but that it might be made navigable without the lead Injury to the adjoining Lands; for that the Lands in general rife about Eighteen Feet above the Surface of the Rivers. Then,

Mr. Robert IV/lfon, Mailer of a Vessel, was examined. Who said he had 11 fed this Navigation for Thirty Years, and that in Floods he had navigated Vessels, laden with Coals and Lime, as high as Topcli/t, but could not do it at low Water: That there are Eight or Nine Shallows in the River, where there is not above Fourteen or Fifteen Inches of Water; and that Persons are obliged to have Vessels with flat Bottoms in order to get over these Shallows, notwithstanding which they frequently drag upon the Ground, and therefore they have Iron Plates fixed to the Bottoms of the Vessels, to prevent them from wearing. And, being asked the distance between the Mouth of the River Swale and Morton Bridge, he said it was about Twenty-eight Miles; That this Navigation will improve the several Estates near or adjoining to it, and will afford the Fanners a better Supply of Manure for Tillage, and at an easier Rate than at present: That, if this Navigation is made, the ex -pence of ‘Carriage of Goods will be greatly reduced, in many Places near one Half, and in others one Third, from what is paid at present; and that the Navigation will be of great Benefit to the Country.

And being asked if he knew the River called Bedale Brook; he laid he did, and had allified very lately in taking the Surveys and Levels of it: That this Brook is both crooked and narrow, and the Fall so great, that without a Canal it is impracticable to make this Navigation.

That the Cut proposed to be made, from Bedale to . Morton Bridge, will be about four miles in Length, which is shorter by about ITiree M iles than the Course of the present river; and that the making this Canal Vot. 31.

will not injure the Lands through which it will be car*

ried. Navigation.

Then Mr. Daxafon,who had surveyed the River Swale and Bedale Brook; and Mr. Gargrave, who had taken the Levels of them; severally gave it as their Opinions, That they are capable of being made navigable, and that such Navigations will be of general utility; and Mr. Dawson delivered in a Plan of the Swale and Bedale Brook, which he had surveyed. Then,

Mr. Alexander Fothergill said, that the Saving in the Price of Carriage, by making this Navigation, will be in general One Third, and in some Cafes One Half, which he explained to your Committee from Calculations he had made. And he added, that he apprehended the Tolls arising upon the River would amount to Two Thousand Pounds per Annum, Then,

Mr. Grundy, an Engineer, was examined; who pro* duced to your Committee an Estimate of the Expence of making the River Swale and Bedale Brook navigable, amounting in the whole to the Sum of^.19,843. 18s. od. and he said, he thought that making the said River and Brook navigable, would be of no Injury to any of the Lands through which the Navigations are proposed to be carried. To prove the Allegations of the last mentioned Petition, for making the Brook called Codbeck navigable,

Mr. Richard Furth was examined; who said he had surveyed that Brook; and he produced a Plan of the intended Navigation, which he explained to your Committee: And he said that the said Brook is about f>even Miles in Length, and that the Fall is Forty-two Feet Eight Inches: That it is practicable to make it a good Navigation, by the Help of Cuts on the Sides of the Brook, and that then the Navigation will be only Five Miles in Length.

That, in order to effect this Navigation it will be ne» celfary to erectsF°ur Locks upon the Brook, the Ex-' i -pence whereof will be about Six thousand One hundred Pounds; and the Land necessary to be purchased will be about Thirty-five Acres; and the annual Expence of maintaining this Navigation will not exceed Twenty Pounds.

And, being asked how' he made his Calculations of the Expence, he said he was afliited in doing it by Mr.

Smith, an Engineer.

Upon being asked the question,hfc said he had been employed in Works of Drainage, but not in Navigations:

That this Navigation will be of Advantage to the Estates in that Part of the Country, and will be of no Injury to any Body.

That the Land through which the Navigation is to be made is rich Pasture and Meadow Land, and is of different Prices: That the Inclosures, through which the Canal is to be carried, are of different Sorts, some large, some small.

That he took this Survey at the Desire of the Gentlemen of Thirsk; but cannot say whether Application had been made to the Proprietors of Lands through which it is proposed to go; but laid it would be of great Benefit to all the Country adjacent, particularly to the

Estates towards Hamilton.

That it will greatly reduce the Price of Carriage of Goods and Merchandize, and of Coals and Manure.

That the road at present is about the same Distance the Navigation Will be when made: That it is a Turnpike Road at present for about a Mile.

A Petition of the Reverend Bobert Smith, Doctor in Hr.ute Divinity, Master of the College of The Holy Trinity, Huntre Fen within the University of Cambridge, and the Fellotvs and Inclosure. Scholars of the same College, Impropriator of the Great Tythes, and Patron of the Vicarage of Swineshead, in the County of Lincoln;the Reverend John Shaw,

Doctor of Law, Patron and Rector of the Parish Church of Wyber'ton, in the County of Lincoln, and Proprietor of I Ioufes, Toftsteads, and Lands, in the said Parish:

Zachary Chambers, Esquire, Lord of the Manor of Swinejhcad, in the said County of Lincoln; Thomas Wyld, Esquire, Lessee, under Trinity College aforesaid, of the Impropriate Tythes of Sioinej aforesaid; and of several Gentlemen and Freeholders, entitled to Right of Common in Haute Huntre Fen, commonly called The Eight Hundred, or Holland Fen, lying in the said County of Lincoln, as Owners and Proprietors of Houses, Toftsteads, and Lands; was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have seen a printed Copy of a Bill, depending in the House; and also certain printed Propositions thereto annexed, respecting the Framing and Modelling the said Bill, for the Purpose of dividing and inclosing the said Fen; and that the Petitioners are greatly diflotisfied with the hasty Method which hath been uied in bringing the said Bill into the House; and apprehend, that a Survey, or Plan of the said Fen, and a Return of the several Houses, Toftsteads, and Lands, within the several Parishes and Hamlets which have Right of Common on the said Fen, ought to have been made, previous to the bringing in the said Bill, in order to enable the Proprietors to judge which of the different Modes offered to them, by the said Propositions, will be productive of th® most equitable Division of the said Fen; and that, on the 16th Day of October 1766, at a Public Meeting of several of the Proprietors entitled to Right of Common in the said Fen, at Sleaford, in the said County of Lincoln, in pursuance of an Advertisement /or that Purpose, a Bill for dividing and inclosing the said Fen was, by some of the said Proprietors then present, proposed to be read; but the Reading thereof was objected to by a great Majority of the said Proprietors then present, infilling that a Plan, or Survey, of the said Fen, ought then to have been produced and laid before the Proprietors at that Meeting, agreeable to a printed Agreement advertised, as the Resolutiou of several Gentlemen and others, Part of the aforesaid Proprietors, at a Meeting held at the Angel

Inn,at Sleiford,in the said County, on the 26th Day of

August, 1766; and that no such Plan, or Survey, being then produced, the aforesaid Majority requeued, and infilled, that all further Proceedings relating to the intended Diviiiou of the said Fen might Hop, until the then next Spring; but, notwithstanding the said Re-quell, some few of the said Proprietors, then present, proposed that a Petition for the said Bill might then be signed; which Proportion being rejected by a considerable Majority, the said few Proprietors declared their Resolution to sign such a Petition, as soon as their then Meeting was broke up, and which laid Meeting did soon afterwards break up without any Resolutions being concluded upon,.pr the Sentiments of the Majority of the Proprietors either entered down or paid any Regard to,

and without making any Adjournment of the said Meeting; and that., soon after the said Meeting broke tip, fonie of the Proprietors present at the said Meeting ffgned the Petition, in conl'cquence of which the said Bill hath been brought in; and that the said Petition appears to be signed by a very few Proprietors, other than such as relide within the Parish of Weji; and that there are Eleven Parishes interested in the Division of the said Fen, several of which are very large and populous; and that the Petitioners arewilling to concur in any Measures, or Proposals, which may be productive of an equitable Division of the said Fen; and conceive that no Injury, or Damage, can accrue to any Person interested in the said Fen, in case the said Bill be not further proceeded on until the next Session; and that the Estates of the Proprietors, inter-efted in the said Fen, amount to ^'.20,000 a Year, and upwards; and that the said Fen is very extensive and fertile, and succours large Quantities of Cattle throughout the whole Year; and, as several of the said Parishes lie very remote from the said Fen, the Petitioners conceive, that if a Plan, or Survey, of the said Fen, as aforesaid, be made and taken, for the previous Satisfaction and Information of the Proprietors, and a further Time be given to the Proprietors to consider and judge of the said intended Division, and the proper Mode for making such Division, it will produce Unanimity in the Proprietors; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the said Bill is in many Places very exceptionable: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, as it now Hands; and that they may have such other Relief as shall seem meet.

A Petition of the MayOr and Commonalty and Citizens of the City of London.

And then they withdrew.

And the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Petition of the Trustees appointed to put in Execution an Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of his late Majesty, for ascertaining, preferring, and improving, the Navigation of the River Lee, hath been presented to the House, for a Bill for further improving the Navigation of the said River; and that, by an Act, passed in the Thirteenth Year of Queen Elizabeth, the Petitioners w'ere impowered to make the new Cut, or River, mentioned in the said Petition, within which the Trustees, appointed by the said Statute of the Twelfth Year of his late Majesty, have no Power to act:

And that the Improvement of the Navigation of the River Lee, from the Town of Hertford, to the River Thames, being an Object of very great Importance to the City of London, and to Trade, the Petitioners are desirous of doing every Thing in their Power to promote the fame; and, with that View, if it Ihonld appear to the House to be necessary, that the w hole Navigation should be committed to the Care of the same Trustees, the Petitioner^ are content to wave their Claim to any exclusive Power, or Jurisdiction, over any Part thereof, saving all other their Rights, Liberties, and Franchises; and that the Petitioners are Proprietors of certain Estates lying near to the said River, and of several Mills, and Mill Streams, wrhich are supplied with Water from the said River, all which may be greatly allotted and prejudiced by the Improvements mentioned in the said Petition being carried into Execution: And therefore praying. That, if Leave should be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition, Provision may be made therein for the Security and Indemnity of the Petitioners, and their Tenants, of the said Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Committee of Merchants trading to Africa, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have laid before the House an Account of the Sum granted for 1765, examined and passed by the Curfitor Baron of the Exchequer, as required by an Act passed in the Year 1750, for extending and improving the Trade to Africa; and that they have expended the Money granted in 1766, for the Support of the several Forts upon the Coast of Africa, in Goods, Stores, and Necessaries; and the Petitioners, being sensible of the great Regard shewn by the House for the British Forts and Settlements upon the Coast of Africa, therefore pray the House to grant such a Sum for the necessary Support thereof for the ensuing Year, as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

was made from the Committee, who were appointed to prepare an Estimate of the Charge of the Pay and Clothing of the Militia, in that Part of Great Britain called England, and the Amount of 28 Days Subsistence for the Commission Officers of the said Militia, under the Rank of Major, for One Year, beginning the 25th Day of March 1767, be referred to tire said Committee;

and although the said Road and Bridge, by the Indulgence of the Petitioner’s PredCceftors, have been long laid open for common and public Ule, yet, until the said Piece of Meadow Ground was converted into a Wharf, the Resort of Passengers and Carriages was so ineonliderable, that they were capable of being maintained in good Repair at a very small Expence; and fhat the said Wharf is situated about the Middle of the said Road, and all Carriage^, going to or coming from the said Wharf, constantly pass along the fame; and by the Increase of the Business of the said Navigation of late Years, the Resort of Carriages upon the said Road and Bridge is become so great and frequent, that the fame, cannot be repaired without a conllant and a very large Expence; and that the Petitioner^and his immediate Predeceflfor, have laid out several Hundred Pounds in the Repair of the said Road, notwithstanding which, the same is now in a very ruinous Condition, and, by the further Increase of Trade on the said River, which will be the Consequence of the said Bill, the Expence of repairing the same will be also proportionably increased; and that as the great Expence of repairing the said Road is occasioned by the many heavy Carriages passing to and from the said Wharf, the Petitioner apprehends the Proprietors of the said Navigation should take upon themselves the Repair of the said Road, to which the Petitioner is willing to contribute such Annual Sum as to the House shall appear reasonable: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and that Provision may be made in the said Bill for granting him such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.
