Mr. Peter Roberts, Comptroller of the Bridgehouse Lands, being examined, said. That London Bridge is subject to a prescriptive Toll upon Carriages passing, coming to, or going out of the said City, loaden with (roods or Provisions; which Toll is appropriated to the Support of the said Bridge, and is at this Time let out upon a Leal’e for 21 Years, from 1765, at

the yearly Rent of £. 735. and a Fine of£. 2,100.

And the said Mr Montagu,being further examined,

said, That he had made a Calculation of the Sum neeeffary for redeeming the said Toll (which Calculation he delivered in to your Committee, and is hereunto . annexed) N° 3.

And the said Mr. Mylne,being furtherexamined, said. That the Passage over London Bridge is sometimes ob-

# o o

ltrufted by Disputes about the said Toll, and was more so while the Toll thereof, under the late Act of Parliament, fubfnted, which Obstructions would beTenTimes greater, upon a Bridge where the Toll extends to Foot Passengers as well as Carriages and Horses; and that he has fecn Instances of the Inconveniences of collecting the Toll upon the Temporary Bridge at Black Fryars, which occasions great Obstructions; and the Collectors have been insulted, and even knocked down, in the Execution of their Duty.

And the said Mr. Mylne, being farther examined, laid. That several Wharfs on the North Sideof the said River, between Paul's Wharf and Milford , projecting . one before another, form an irregular and disagreeable Outline, and give the Proprietors of some of them, of course, an Advantage over others.

That the reflected Set of the Tides, both of Ebb and Flood, throws the Force of the Stream upon the Surrey Shore, opposite to Black Fryars, and thereby lladkens the Current upon the London Side, which, together with the Sewers that empty themselves into the RiVer in that Neighbourhood, occasions a constant Accumulation of Sand, Mud, and Rubbish, and thereby destroys great Part of the Navigation at Low Water, and renders the Wharfs inaccessible by the loaded Craft even at High Water; that this might in great Measure be remedied by embanking that Part of the River, which would be of no Detriment to the Navigation thereof) as it would only occupy a Place that is now filled with Still Water; and although it will advance the Fronts of the Wharfs to that Part of the Stream which has some Degree of Motion, yet it will not increase the Rapidity of the River in any Part of it, mea-furing aero Is the River at that Place, but the Mouths of the Sewers being advanced along with the Wharfs, they will empty themselves in a Part of the Stream, whole Rapidity w ill hinder fu'ch Matter from being accumulated as heretofore, and will diffuse it more generally throughout the River; that the Expence of the said embanking will amount to £.7,511. 14*. for which Sum the Witness said he w ould undertake to do it; that his Method of doing it would be, to begin at each End of the intended Embankment, and to fill up VOL. 31.

the vacant Space, and as that advaheed, to build the Wharf Wall.

Mr. William Robinson, Surveyor to the Trustees of the Grc/hamEstate, being examined, said, That the

Royal Exchange was erected soon after the Fire of London in 1666; that he has lately examined into the State and Condition of the Building, and finds it in very bad Repair; that the Timbers are all decayed, and have been obliged to belhored up for many Years; that. the Estimate he has made of the Expence of an effectual and substantial Repair, amounts to £. 10,020.

Mr. Can me, Clerk to the Mercers Company, being

examined, said. That the present State of the Revenues appropriated for Support of the Royal Exchange are greatly diminished, so as by no means to afford such a Sum as£. 10,000. to be laid out upon it.

Mr. Ford, Clerk of the Gaol Delivery, being examined, said. That the Gaol of is the County

Gaol for London and Middlefand may be looked upon as the Gaol of the whole Kingdom, in re'pest to Smugglers, State Prisoners, and Pirates, and for Debto: -to the Crown.

Mr. Aker man. Keeper of Newgale, being examined, said. That there is no Area or Yard in the said Gaol for Prisoners to walk in; that the whole is very irregularly built; that the Air has no free Passage through any Part, except over the Gateway; that there is no Room or Place for Water, most of the Water being obliged to be pumped from a Reservoir in Newgate Street-, that the Consequence thereof is very bad, and produces the Gaol Distemper; that there are more Prisoners in Proportion lick now than formerly used to be; that the Common Side for Debtors and the Men and Women Felons is so dark, that they are obliged to use Links, Lamps, or Candles all the Year round; and the Witness remembers, some Years ago, at the Old , Two of the Judges, the Lord Mayor, and several of the Jury, to the Number of Sixty Perl'ons or upwards, died of the Gaol Distemper; that he has had near Two Sets of Servants died since he has been Keeper, and moll of them from the Gaol Distemper; that the Neighbours frequently complain in warm Weather of {he Air draw n from the said Gaol by the Ventilator; and that the Walls of the Prison are so bad and thin, that the Prisoners are not secure.

The said Mr. Mylne being again examined, said. That the said Gaol is so old and ruinous, that it is not capable of any Improvement or tolerable Repair; and that the Expence of rebuilding the said Gaol on a more extended Plan, with the necessary Purchases to be made, Additions to the present Sessions House, and all other incidental Expences, will amount to £. 50,000.

Then an Act made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of King William and Queen Mary, intituled, An Act for the Relief of the Orphans, and other Creditors of the City of London, was read, whereby it appeared, that towards raising a perpetual Fund to pay the Interest of the Money then due to the Orphans and other Creditors of the said City, all and every the City’s Estates and Revenues were changed for ever with the clear annual Sum of £. 8,000, the Rents and Profits of the said City’s Aquaedufts, the Sum of £. 2,000, to be annually raised upon the personal Estates of the several Inhabitants wfithin the said City and Liberties, the Sum of 2 6 d.

to be paid upon the binding of every Apprentice within the said City, and 5 s.by every Person admitted a Freeman thereof, were appropriated to the said Fund, as also a Duty of 4s. per Ton upon all Sorts of Wine imported into the Port of the said City, or Members thereof, by way of Merchandize, a Duty of 4 d. fors Metage for every Chaldron of Coals or Culm imported into the said Port or River of Thames within the Liberty of the said City to be sold, and from the 29th Day of September 1700, for and during the Term of 50 Years, a further Duty of 6d. for every Chaldron or Ton of Coals or Culm so imported.

GEORGE R.

H is Majesty having, at the Close of the last Session of Parliament, signified to this House, His Intention of recommending to their Consideration the making of some proper Provision for the honourable Support and Maintenance of his dearly beloved Brothers, the Dukes of York, GLntaftrr, and Cumberland j and having the re-

upon received the Assurance of His faithful Commons, that they would readily and chearfully take the same into their Consideration whenever His Majesty should please to recommend it; and being persuaded that this House will think it reasonable that foine more competent Provision should be made for the honourable Support and Maintenance of His Majesty’s Brothers, than the pro font necessary Charges upon the Civil List have permitted His Majesty to make for that Purpose, as well as that such Provision may be secured to them in such Manner as has been usually done with respect to the several Branches of the Royal Family, is desirous that an Annuity of Eight thousand Pounds per Annum be settled upon each of His Three Brothers, during their relpettive Lives; and His Majesty recommends the Coulideration thereof to this House.

Parish Mr. Whitworth reported from the Committee, ap-

Infant Poor, pointed to inquire into the State of the Parish Poor In-

fants, under the Age of Fourteen Years, within the Bills of Mortality; and to report their Opinion to the I Ioufe; That the Committee had inquired accordingly; and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table.

And a Member returned upon a new Writ, having taken the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and taken and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration; and having delivered iti to the Clerk of this House an Account of his Qualification, and having taken and subscribed the Oath of Qualification; according to the Laws made for those Purposes;

The said Report was read; and is as followeth; viz.

The Committee having examined the Registers of the several Parishes referred to them by the 1 Ioufe, have collected from them the State of the Parish Infant Poor; and find,

ill. That taking the Children born in Workhouses, or Parish Houses, or received of and under Twelve Months old, in the Year 1763, and following the same into 1764 and 1765, only Seven in a Hundred appear to have survived this short Period.

idly. That having called for the Registers of the Years 1754, 1755, 1761, 1762, of the Children placed out Apprentices by the Parishes within the Bills of Mortality, it appears that there have been apprenticed, out, the Number of 1419; but upon examining the Ages at which the said Children so placed out were received, in the Seven Years from 1741, till they grew up to be placed out, it appears that only Nineteen of those born in the Workhouses, or received into them under Twelve Months old, compose any Part of the 1419; and even of those received as far as Three Years old, only Thirty-six appear to have survived in the Hands of the said Parishes to be placed out Apprentice.

3dly. It appears that the Children are kept in the several Workhouses in Town, or in the Hands of Parish Nurses in Town, only a small Portion of them being sent into the Country to be nursed; and the Price of 35. and zs. 6d. per Week first paid, is often reduced so low as i£. 6 d.and is.per Week, that it cannot be presumed to be equal to the necessary Care of Infants.

4tldy. Your Committee find, the Conduct of Parish Nurses was taken notice of by Parliament in the Year 1715, as appears from the Report in the Journals of the House, of the 8th of March in the above Year; Part of which being read, is as follows;

" That a great many poor Infants and expo fed Bastard " Children are inhumanly fuft'ered to die by the Barbarity of Nurses, who are a Sort of People void of Commiseration or Religion, hired by the Churfti Wardens " to take off a Burthen from the Parish at the cheapclt " and easiest Rates they can, and these know, the Man-. " ner of doing it effectually."

And upon examining also into the recent Facts above related, it doth not appear to your Committee that the Evil is or can be remedied, unless proper Regulations are established by legislative Authority.

5thly. It appears from the Evidence of the Parish Officers of Saint Andreio's Iiolborn(called within the City

Liberties) and also from Mr. Hutton, a principal Inhabitant of that Parish, that the Sum of zs. 6d. a Week for the Article of Nursing, is as little as a Child can be nursed at, to have Justice done it; but at the same time, they being fenlible of the good Conduct and Management of the Hospital for the Maintenance and Education of exposed and deserted young Children, they h ve proposed to the Governors and Guardians thereof to receive their Infant Parish Poor at a certain Rate, which by the Minutes of the General Court of the said Hospital, dated the 18th of February 1767, which was produced to your Committee, and read, the said Governors

While

hors and Guardians are ready to comply with, and like-wife to forward any general Purpose the Legislaturemay think proper to direct, in relation to the Preservation of the Infant Parish Poor within the Bills of Mortality.

6thly, It appears, upon the Examination of Saunders Welsh, Esquire, that great Inconveniences have been found from Parish Boys being placed out Apprentice so long as till the Age of Twenty-four. And upon reading the Clause in the 43d of Eliz. Cap. 2. intituled, An Act for the Relief of the Poor; in the 5th Sec. thereof it is said, " Parish Officers are to bind their " Man Child to the Age of Twenty-four, but the " Woman Child to the Age of Twenty-one, or Time of Marriage." This, your Committee think checks Marriage, and discourages Industry.

7thly. It appears to your Committee, that the usual Sum given by Parities with Apprentices, has been generally from ao to 4or. only, which your Committee think inadequate to the procuring good Mailers.

8thly. It appears that the Register directed to be made out by the Act of the Second of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for keeping a regular,

" uniform, and annual Register of all Parish Poor In-" fants under a certain Age, within the Bills of Mortality," is deficient, by not fettingforth how Children are disposed of after the Age of Four Years.

Upon the Whole, your Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Parish Infant Poor, within the Bills of Mortality, should be sent into the Country to be nursed, at a Distance, not less than a certain Number of Miles, from any Part of the Town.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Parish Officers should allow and pay a certain Sum for nursing each Child.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a proper Number of principal Inhabitants should be chosen in every Parish respectively, under the Denomination of Guardians of the Parish Infant Poor, to inspect into the Treatment of the said Children, nursed as above.

Re/'olved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Parish Officers, Governors, and Directors of the Poor, should have the Alternative of fending such Children to the Hospital for the Maintenance and Education of exposed and defferted young Children; and the Governors and Guardians thereof be permitted to take them at a certain Sum, and to be paid by the said Officers for nurling such Children out of the Parish Rates.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Parish Children should be placed out Apprentice for a shorter Time than is by Law prescribed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a proper Sum should be given, as Apprentice Fees, with the said Parish Children.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Register of Infant Poor, under Four Years of Age, should be continued on, till the Children are in some Manner disposed of in the World.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severallyput thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Sir Joseph Mawbet/ reported from the Committee, to

whom the Petition of several Merchants, His Majesty’s British Subjects, concerned in the Whale Fishery, on behalf of themselves and others concerned in the said Fishery; and also the Petition of the Royal Boroughs of Scotland, met at Edinburgh, the 30th Day o(January 1767; were severally referred; That the Commit-Vol. 31.

tee had examined the Matter Of Facl contained in the said Petitions; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

A State of the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petitions, is as follows:

By an Act of the Sixth Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, for the further Encouragement of the Whale Fishery, after reciting the Provisions made by Two former Acts, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his Majesty King George the First, and the Fifth Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, and that the Whale Fins, Oil, and Blubber, taken in the Greenland Seas or Davis’s Straits, and the adjacent Seas, in British Sfiips, and imported by British Subjects, should be free of Customs,

on the Conditions therein mentioned: And, after a Recital that the said Encouragements had been by many Years Experience found insufficient for the regaining of this beneficial Trade, which M as then in great Danger of being utterly loft; and that large Quantities of Oil and Whale Fins were at a great Expence bought of Foreigners, and Annually imported into this Kingdom: It is enacted, that, on the Conditions in the said Act mentioned, the Commissioners of the Customs in England or Scotland respectively should, on Demand, cause Payment to be made to the Mailer or Owners of every Ship employed in the said Fishery, according to the Directions of the said Act, or to his or their Assigns, by the Receiver General of the Customs for that Part of Great Britain from whence the Ship departed, the Sum of 2o r. per Ton, according to the Admeasurement of such Slip, duly certified, as in the said A ft is directed: And, by an Act made-in the Thirteenth Year of his late Majesty, afurther Bounty of 1 or. per Ton was granted for all Ships employed in the Whale Fishery during the then present War.

And, by an Act made in the Twenty-second Year of his said late Majesty's Reign, for the further Encouragement and Enlargement of the Whale Fishery, the said Acts, made in the Fifth, Sixth, and Thirteenth Years of his late Majesty’s Reign, were further continued to the 25th Day o f Dece 1757; and by the same Act, over and above the Allowance of 20 a Ton, an additional Bounty was granted upon every Ship, payable in like Manner as -in the said Act is directed.

And by another Act, made in the Twenty-eighth Year of his said late Majesty, after reciting that several Acts had been made for the Encouragement of his Majesty’s Subjects to carry on and improve the Whale Fishery, the said several Acts herein before mentioned were continued, and also the said additional Bounty, unto the 25th Day o fDecember 1764, and to the End of the then next Session of Parliament.

And by another Act, made in the Fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, after reciting the said several Acts, and that the Bounties given thereby had (till checked by the late War) greatly increased the said Fishery, to the Advantage of the Trade and Navigation of these Kingdoms; the said Acts, and the Bounty of 40V. a Ton thereby granted, were further continued, from the 25 th Day of December 1764 to the 25th Day of December 1767, and to the End of the then next Session of Parliament.

And, from several Accounts presented to this House for several Years last past, by the Commissioners of His Majesty's Customs, it appeared to your Committee, that this Trade had greatly increased, particularly since the passing of the Act of the Twenty-second of his late Majesty, until the breaking out of the Jate War; there having been employed, as your Committee were informed, preceding the granting the per Ton Bounty, only Three Ships on a Medium in a Year;

But it appears from the Accounts,

That, in the Year 1756, Sixty-seven Ships were fit-3 S ted

ted out from E?igland] and Sixteen Ships from Scotland, upon this Fishery; by which Means upwards of 4,000 Seamen must have been in that Year, and nearly the same Number the preceding Year, employed in this Fishery; but that, after the Commencement of the War, that Trade had gradually declined.

And, by the Evidence of Mr. James Mather, Mr. Henri) Bird, and Mr. Campier, it appeared to your Committee, that, at the End of the War, the Bounty being nearly expiring, no Person would venture to engage in this Trade, without a further Continuance of the Bounty; and therefore, in the Fourth Year of His present Majesty, an Act of Parliament was made for further continuing the Bounty '; but, the Term of this Act being only for Three Years, and to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, it was not long enough to encourage the Owners of Ships to fit them out lor this Trade: That, the Charge of fitting out Ships being double in this Trade to what it is in any other, if, after being so fitted out, they lliould be obliged to go into any other Trade, there would be a Loss to the Owners of £. 75 perCent. upon every Ship, as the Fishing Materials, being the most considerable Part of the Expence, would be almost intirely thrown away.

That, if the Bounty was continued for the further Term of Seven Years, they apprehended 100 Sail of Ships at the least, from England, would be employed in this Fishery; and that, as they always got One Third of Landmen to go in these Ships, this Fishery was a very great Nursery for Seamen: And the Reason they gave for having OneThird Landmen was, that, besides the Act of Parliament’s obliging them to carry an Apprentice for every 50 Tons Burthen, the Officers,

1 Iarponeers, S'c. were so expensive, that they could not afford a compleat Ship’s Company of Sailors: And they said, that (he Number of Men necessary for a Ship in this Service was 50; and that the Men employed therein arc allowed, by all Nations, to be the hard fell in the World: And the Witnesses said, that, if the Bounty was not continued, this Trade mull be intirely at a Stand.

And that we formerly purchased all the Utensils for

this Fishery from Foreigners; but now they are made at Home, and are better than the Dutch can make them; and are a very considerable Branch of Trade at Whitby and Birmingham; and many Manufacturers are employed in making Harpoons, Lances, Lines, &'c.

That, if the Bounty was given on the Fish caught, it would not encourage Persons to engage in this Trade, and would not be so beneficial to the Country as if granted upon the Ships; as a Bounty of that Sort would be payable upon the small Fish as well as the great; and they added, that a Bounty of 305*. a Tou would not be sufficient to encourage this Fishery, as had been already experienced.

And, by the Evidence of Mr. Mather, it appeared . to your Committee, that the Price of Whale Bone had been for feme Years past from £. 260 to £. 300, and that it is now £. 510 a Ton; and that, if the Bounty is not continued, it may rife /. 10o or £.200 a Ton higher than at present, as the Dutch now keep it up till they know the Fate of this Application; and, if this Bounty is not continued, our Ships must be fitted out from Holland, as they can be fitted out £. 30 per Cent. cheaper there than at Home; and One of the Witnesses said, he would fend his Clerk to settle a House there, and fit out his Ships from thence.

Then your Committee inquired into the State of the American Fishery; and it appeared to them, from the Evidence of the Witnesses, that lall Year had been very unfavourable to that Fishery, they having caught only 14 Whales.

That the Greenland Bone and the American differ greatly in their Nature, the Greenland being much better, and being £. 50 a Ton higher Price at Market.

That the Americanyone will not work like the Greenland; it is in its Nature more brittle.

That One of the Witnesses this Year has imported Seven Tons of Bone from Holland; and fays, if the Bounty is not continued, he apprehends he shall have 20 Tons consigned to him in the Course of the Year.

A Petition of several of the Commissioners for putting London in Execution an Act made in the last Session of Parlia- Paving; ment, for paving the Streets and Lanes, within the Town and Borough of Southwark, and certain Parts ad- oa uue,‘ jacent, in the County of Surrey, and for cleansing, lighting, and watching the fame, and also the Courts, Yards,

Alleys, and Passages adjoining thereto, and for preventing Annoyances therein; and of several of the Inhabitants, Merchants, Tradesmen, and others, of the said Town and Borough, and Parts adjacent; was presented ed to the House, and read 5 Setting forth. That the Petitioners, the Commissioners, have proceeded to put the said Act in Execution, and have, pursuant to the Powers thereby given, erected Turnpikes, and do collect the Sundays Tolls thereby granted, asaFundto raise Money upon, for the more expeditiously paving the Streets, and other Places, within the said Town and Borough and Parts adjacent; and have taken up at Interest, on the Credit of the said Tolls, as much Money as the same will properly bear, which has been duly, and with the utmost Frugality and strictest Oeconomy, applied according to the Directions of the said Act, and great Progress has been made in paving the said Streets; but, as the Rate authorized by the said Act to be collected is not more than sufficient to pay the Expence of lighting, watching, deanfing, regulating, and repairing the said Streets, and other Places, within the said Borough, the Petitioners find themselves unable, under the Powers of the said Act, to raise Money sufficient to complete the Works directed by the said Act to be done; and that it appears, by the Votes of the House, that Application is making to Parliament, for an Act to extend, for a Term of Years, the Duty of Four Pence and Sixpence per Chaldron on Coals and Culm imported into the Port of London, laid by an Act of the Fifth and Sixth Years of King William and Queen Mary, and continued by an Act of the Twenty-first of King George the Second, and to apply the same in regulating the Wharfs, repairing the Royal Exchange, and performing other Works within the said City, and likewifein re-building Newgate, the County Gaol for Middlesex; and that the Petitioners acknowledge that the said Works will be of great Use and Advantage to the said City of London and County of Middlesex, but at the fameTime presume, that the Works by the said Act of last Session directed to be performed within the Town and Borough of Southwark, and Parts adjacent, are also Works of public Nature, equal with those proposed to be done in London; and that a very considerable Proportion of the above-mentioned Duties is paid by the Inhabitants of the fiaid.

Town and Borough of Southwark, and Places adjacent in the County of Surrey, there being many Brewers,

Glass Makers, Distillers, Dyers, Founders, and others, -.

uling immense Quantities of Coals, in their several Manufactures and Businesses settled there; wherefore the Petitioners humbly presume that it will be thought reasonable, that if the said Duties upon Coals be further continued, a moderate Proportion of the Money to be raised thereupon should be applied for the Purposes of completing the public Works of paving within the said Town and Borough of Southwark and Parts adjacent:

« But they are notwithstanding of Opinion, that Application should be marie to Parliament, for Leave to " pay the said Mr. John Harrison, upon his producing " his Time Keeper to certain Persons to be named by this Board, and discovering to them the Principles and Manner of making the same, so much Money " as w ill make up the Sums already advanced to him,

And the said Mr. WillilimHarrifon, being examined, informed your Committee, That he performed a Voyage to the West Indies, in order to make a Trial of this Time Keeper, by Direction of the Commissioners of Longitude:

That he arrived at Barbadoes the 13th of May, and returned home the 18th of July, 1764:

That his Father has received 10,000 as a Public Reward for the Discovery of this Time Keeper, besides some other Money for Experiments:

That the lull Payment of this Money was made on the 28th of October 1765, when he delivered his Time Keeper to the Commissioners of Longitude, ;and received the Sum of £. 7,500:

That prior to this, he had discovered the Principles of his Machine toPersons authorized by the Commissioners of Longitude, to examine him in relation thereto. In Confirmation of which, he produced to your Committee the following Certificate:

" We, whose Names are hereunto subscribed, do " certify, that Mr. John Harrison has taken his Time " Keeper to pieces in the Presence of us, and explained the Principles and Construction thereof, and every " Thing relative thereto, to our entire Satisfaction; and " that he also did, to our Satisfaction, answer to every " Question proposed by us, or any of us, relative thereto; and that wre have compared the Drawings of the " same with the Parts; and do find that they perfectly " correspond.

Then he informed your Committee, that these Drawings and the Explanation have been printed, and were published about the 14th of this Month, and he is of Opinion, that these Drawings and the Explanation are suficient to enable different Workmen to make Time peepers upon his Principle, that will answer the Purposes thereby intended.

Mr. Tho'. Mudge, a Watchr Maker, being examine^, said, that he was One of the Persons that received this Discovery of Mr. Harrison's Machine.

That the Drawings and Descriptions, given by Mr. Harrison to the Board, he thinks, would not enable a Workman to make such a Machine; but from the further Infiruftions given to him by Mr. Harrison, he is now able to make them as well as Mr. Harrison himself.

Being alked. Whether a suficient Number of these Time Keepers could not be made, so as to be of general Uie to the Public ? -

He said, that he thinks not; for-in the present State of Mechanism in this Kingdom, there is a great Scarcity of good Workmen in the Watch-making Business.

Being alked. What he knew in relation to any French Artist having discovered the Principles of this Time Keeper?

He said, that since the Discovery was made to him, he had made no Secret of it, but had explained the Principles to every Mechanic that alked him about it, and amongst others, toMonfieur who

is a Watch-maker at Paris, and who was in iu

February last, when the Witness gave him the bell Account he could of this Time Keeper; and he has lately had reason to think, that Monsieur Barthaud came to England to discover the Principles of this Machiue.

That Monlieur LeMonier, another ofhisCorrefpon-dents at Paris, informs him, that a Premium has been offered there for Marine Watches, or Watches for finding the Longitude at Sea; in consequence of which, feme Marine Watches have been delivered in; that Mr. Barthaud appeared at this Competition after having been privately at Londons but that some other Competitors have succeeded better than he, particularly Monsieur Le Roy, who has made a Marine Watdi, which he (Monsieur Le Monier) has tried, and found to be very exact; but does not say what Trial he has made, nor the Degree of Exactness.

He then produced a Letter from Monsieur Barthaud, dated at Paris the 2d of February last, wherein he Informs him, that Monsieur Le Roy has made a Marine Watch; and that he is not the only one who is aiming at the Discovery; and since the Knowledge of the Suc-cefe of Mr. Ilarrifon, and the Reward given him, every little Watch-maker is endeavouring to make Marine Watches; and we shall fee what this Fermentation will produce.

Ordered, That the Lord CVare do make the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the present high Price of Com.

The Lord Clare accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed to be reported to the House; which he read in his Place} and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read} and are as followeth; vix.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Price of Com is, in many Places, frequently enhanced by the present System of Laws, relating to Badgers, Engrossers, Forestallers, and Regraters.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved, that a Committee be appointed to consider of the said Laws; and to report their Opinion to the House, which are fit to be continued, amended, or repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Importation of any Sort of Com, Grain, or Meal, which is allowed by any Act of this Session of Parliament, be admitted for a further limited Time, free of Duty.

Tl*fe First Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Second Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed to consider of the Laws relating to Badgers, Engrossers, Forestallers, and Regraters; and to report their Opinion to the House, which of the same are fit to be continued, amended, or repealed.

Whereupon your Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Children belonging to the Foundling Hospital, be placed out Apprentices, to Husbandry, Manufactures, or to the Sea, or other Service, as soon as the Ages and Abilities of such Children shall admit of it, and proper Mailers and MistrelTes can be provided for them.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there may be allowed to every Mailer or Millrefs who shall take any such Apprentice, upon the Terms hereafter mentioned, a Sum of Money, at the Discretion of such Governors and Guardians(having regard to the Age, Sex and Ability of each Child) not exceeding the Maintenance of such Child for One Year, to be paid at such Time or Times, and in such Portions, as shall be agreed upon between the Governors and Guardians and the Master or Millrefs for that Purpose.

BeJ'olved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, that noMaleChildlhould be bound longer than until his Age of 21 Years, and that no Female Child should be bound longer than her Age of 21, or Marriage; and that the Mailer or Millrefs should be obliged by proper Covenants to find and provide such Apprentice all necessary Clothes, Provisions, and Inltruftions, during the Time of their respective Apprenticeships.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Air. James Fordham,being examined, said, That the

present Navigation is very incommodious; that a light Barge is sometimes Three Days in making a Trip, and sometimes Five; and that a loaded Barge is sometimes a Fortnight,

That they are frequently flopped by the Shallow?, particularly at WalthamGull, which is about a Alile from Mr. Walton's Mills; that they get over this by Means of a great Body of Water, which in dry Seatons must come from Hertford, with the Addition of Mr. Walton’s

Wafer, which Assistance they can commonly haveTwice a Week; but in very dry Seasons only Once:

That the Hated Days for this Supply of Water are Wednesdaysand Sundays, but in lhort Water Times, Sundays only; so that if a Barge happens to be flopped on a Sunday, it mull necessarily lie there till the Wednesday, if not, till the Sunday following; but that they are never refused Water on a Sunday, even for a Angle Barge:

That the next Shallow is at Eaton’s Wear* where he has known Barges flopped for a Fortnight, and by putting a-breast of each other, they have flopped all the Barges on the Stream; and that they are supplied with Water at the same Times, and in the same Manner here as at the Waltham Gull:

That there are no other Shallows on the River so bad as those abovementioned; but there are several other Places where Barges are obliged to wait for Flaflies: ' That between Hertford and the River Thames, there are near Thirty Weirs, or Turnpikes, at which the BargemaHers pay 59 s.in the common Course of Water; and that when Barges get to the Alouth of the River Lee, if the Wind is at South West, they sometimes lie for a Week before they can get into the River Thames:

That Bargemasters pay for Water at the Will of the Owners of Alills; and that by these several Discouragements, the Number of Barges on this River is decreased, Laqd Carriage being sometimes cheaper than Water Carriage; and that Flour is now commonly Tent by Land, which, if the Navigation w’as certain, would all go by Water:

That Barges carry 35 Tons down, and upon an Average not more than 10 Tons up the River.

Mr. Jonathan Jackson, a Barge-Mailer, being., examined, confirmed Air. Fordham’s Evidence, and added. That he has sometimes been denied Water by. the Proprietors of Wears.

That he has frequently been detained at the Mouth of the River Lee; and that when a Barge gets into the River Thames there, lhe cannot get up to London in One Tide When the Wind is fair and high.:

- Air. Thomas Marlborough, a Miller at Hertford, being examined, said. That he finds great Inconveniences from the present State of the Navigation; that he used to fend Flour by Water, but as he cannot depend on its being delivered in time, he has lent it by Land for many Years: That if the Navigation was good, it would reduce the Price of Carriage, and consequgntly would be advantageous both to the City of London, and the Country.

Air. James Rondeau, a Cornfactor ’in London, said. That the Improvement of the Navigation will be very beneficial to the City of London, as Inconveniences frequently happen by Corn being Hopped on the present Navigation.

Mr. Yeomans, being again examined, said, That the Navigation will be rendered much more safe, lhort, and commodious by the proposed Plan; and that occasional Supplies of Water from the Mills will then, beunuecef-Yol. 31.

fary: That the Navigation from Bromley Mills to Lime- River Le« honj'e Hole, is at present about Nine Miles, and the Navigation, proposed Canal will be no more than €)nc Mile, One Quarter, and Thirty-one Poles; and by Means of this Cut, the Communication with the River Thames will be so much nearer London, that Barges will get up in One Tide; and that a Barge will be enabled to go from the e Town of Hertford to the River Thames, and return . again in 28 Hours j and that at present Barges arb obliged to wait for Ebb and Flood Tides to go up and down Bozo Creek, which now requires Two Tides; but by the proposed Canal, this Inconvenience will be remedied, and tluyewill be noNecelfity to wait for Tides.

That he has made Companion between the Expence of Carriage on the present and on the proposed Navigation: That at present Three Men and One Boy are employed to navigate a Barge, which makes about Forty Trips in a Year; that their Wages each Trip is £.6. 8*. which'is £ 256 a Y'ear for navigating One Barge: That upon the proposed Navigation, Two Men and One Boy will be able to navigate a Barge, which may make Five Trips backwards and forwards in a Fortnight; and the Wages for each Trip will be £.2. xor. The Number of Trips each Year will con-l'equently be 130, and the Wages £. 300.

That a Barge now carries about 300 Quarters of Alalt down the River, and about Eight Tons, or Chal? drons of Coals up; so that the whole Quantity that a Barge can now carry down the River in a Year, is 12,000 Quarters, and the back Carriage 320 Tons; oij. the new Navigation, a Barge will bring down 49,000 Quarters per Annum, and carry back 2,600 Tons of other Commodities; and consequently the Carriage in a Barge will be augmented in the Proportion of Three Fourths to One down, and as Eight to One up thq River.

Walton's Alills would beleflened in l’ome Degree, though he cannot precisely say to what Extent, but it would certainly prevent their working iri some Measure; and he looks upon this Turnpike as absolutely necessary for those Mills.

Hemp and Flax.

A Petition of the general Convention of the Royal Boroughs of Scotland, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth; That the Linen and Hempen Manufactures, the Staple of that Part of the United Kingdom, labour under great Hardships, and are not only in Danger of decrealing, but of being totally loll, owing to the high Prices the Manufacturers mult ue-ceflarily pay for foreign Materials, in so much, that there is now given Fifty per Cent, of advanced Price more than was paid for the same Qualities of Hemp and Flax Seven Years ago; and that, besides the Quantities raised at Home, or brought from America, it is believed that Great Britain pays Annually to foreign States not leis than One million. Sterling for Flemp and Flax; and that the Legislaturc lues lately granted a Bounty on the Importation of those Materials from the British Colonies; but it is to be feared, that, by reason of the high Price of Labour in the Colonies, and the high Rates for Freight and Infuranccson inch bulky and valuable Commodities as Hemp and Flax, besides the Damage which those Articles always sustain upon a long Voyage, our Supplies from thence will not be so cheap, so long, or so speedy, as could be willied; it is therefore proposed and requelted* in order to preserve and enlarge our Linen Manufactures, to render our Navigation independent of foreign States, and in Time to preserve to the Nation such a capital Sum as is now annually expended upon foreign Hemp and Flax, that the Parliament would all’o grant a Bounty on the Culture of Flax and Hemp in Great Britain, in such Way and Manner as to the House shall seem proper: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and to grant such Relief therein, as to them shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Navy A Petition of the Lieutenants of His Majesty’s Navy,

Lieutenants, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, in Behalf of themselves and others, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read j Setting forth, That the Petitioners flatter themselves, that, during the Course of the late successful War, they served His Majesty and their Country with the greatest Zeal and Fidelity; and declare themselves ready and ambitious to renew their Services, whensoever the Royal Command, and their Country’s Service, shall again call them into Action; and representing to the House, that their prefrnt Pay is insufficient to l'upport them in any Character as Oflicrrs in His Majesty’s Service; and that great Numbers of the Petitioners, being now reduced to Half Pay, the Amount thereof is so far from being adequate to their Sit nation as Officers, that it will not supply them even singly with the common Necessaries of Life; and many of them, being charged with Families, are particularly labouring under the most mortifying Distrefies: And therefore bcfeeching the House to take the same into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as they 1i1a.ll think meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to v horn it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

A Petition of George Byrd, and James Johnson, Esquires, on Belial f of themselves and the rest of the Proprietors of the Westham Water-Works, in the County of Essex, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners apprehend, if the Bill now depending in the House, lor improving the Navigation of the River Lee, from a certain Place in the Town of Hertford to the River Thames, should pals Vol. 31.

into a Law, as it now stands, great Damage will accrue to their Works, to the Loss and Injury of the Petitioners: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as may affect them, or that they may have such other Relief in the Premiles, as to the House shall appear just and reasonable.

A Petition of James Townsend, Esquire, Lord of the Manors of Tottenham, Pembr Braces, and Mockings, in the County of and of the

several other Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Owners of Lands, and other Estates within the said Manors, and Inhabitants of the Parish of Tottenham, was also prefertted to the House, and read; Setting forth. That there hath been an ancient Navigation for Boats, and other Vessels, along the River Lee, from the Town of Hertford, into the River Thames, in the same Channel where the said River now runs, which extends for a great Length along the said Manors and Parish of Tottenham; and that an Act was passed, in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for improving the said Navigation, whereby it is, amongst other Things, enacted, that the said Navigation should for ever be fixed, and continue in the same Channel, or Course, wherein the said River then run, and was used for Navigation; and that very little, if any thing, hath been done for the Improvement of the said Navigation, in pursuance and Execution of the Powers contained in the said Act; and that the Petitioner James Townsend, is possessed of an ancient Mill, and Mill Stream, in the said Parish of which, from Time to Time immemorial, hath been supplied, and hath a Right to be supplied, with Water from the said River Lee; and that the Petitioners observe by the Votes, that a Bill is brought in for the improving the Navigation of the said River Lee; and that the Petitioners are informed, that it is intended to desert the ancient Course of the said River, and to make sundry new Cuts to the Westward thereof; and that by the Alterations and Improvements proposed by the said Bill, the Petitioners will be greatly injured in their Estates and Properties, and subjected to many Inconveniences: And therefore praying. That they may be heard by themselves, or their Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill which may affect them; and that the Petitioners may be relieved in the Premises, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of James Barwick, on Behalf of liirnfelf, and Mary Farran, Widow, both of Waltham Abbey, in the County of Essex, Callico Printers and Partners, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner, and the said Mary Farran, now do, and for several Years past have carried on the Business of Callico Printers, in Grounds adjoining to the River Lee }and that the Petitioner observes by the

Votes, that a Bill has been brought into the House, for improving the Navigation of the said River Lee, from a certain Place in the Town of Hertford, to the River Thames, and for making divers new Cuts, or Canals, for that Purpose; and that the Petitioner is informed, it is intended to make a Cut, or Canal, out of the said River, from above King's Wear, to or near the West Tail Stream of the Powder Mills, near Waltham Abbey aforesaid, whereby, as the Petitioner apprehends, the Property of the said Mary Farran, and himself, will be greatly affected: And therefore praying, on Behalf of himself, and the said Mary Farran, that they may be heard by their Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as may affect their Interest; and that such Relief may be giver to them in the Premises, as to the House shall seem inset and just.

and Holland, and the Dealers in foreign Linens, from Dunes on those Countries, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, LuieM*46 was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is brought in, for laying additional Duties on divers Sorts of foreign Linens imported into this Kingdom; andre-presenting to the House, that the Trade carried on between England and Germany, and Holland, from whence those Linens are chiefly imported, is very beneficial to this Nation, in regard the Value of the Manufactures of this Kingdom, and of its Colonies, exported to Germany and Holland, greatly exceeds the Imports from thence, and that the Duties payable upon the Importation of foreign Linens into this Kingdom are already very high, the same having increased Ten per Cent, during the Two last Wars with France; but the Produce and Manufactures of Great Britain, and its Colonies, are admitted into Germany and Holland, on very easy Terms; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that in case any additional Duties should be laid on the Species of Linens enumerated in the Votes of the House, the same may occasion Measures to be taken by foreign Powers, which may tend greatly to discourage and lessen the Demand of Woollen and other Goods of British Produce, and may also be attended with other Consequences very prejudi* cial to the Trade of this Kingdom, and greatly increase the Practice of Smuggling: And therefore praying, Tha$ the Petitioners may be heard, against so much of the said Bill, as relates to the laying any additional Duties on foreign Linens imported into this Kingdom, o~ that they may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Under Subscribers, Proprietors of East India Stock; was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of the House, that a Bill is depending for regulating the Dividends of the East India Company; and that the Petitioners are advised, that certain Clauses in the said Bill, as now proposed, if passed into a Law, would prove extremely prejudicial to the Rights and Property of the Petitioners, and would materially affect public Credit in general, as well as the particular Interests of the Company; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the Motives to the Conduct of the Pro-, prietors at their late General Courts, with relation to the Dividend, as well as the Circumstances of the Company, which induced them to vote such a Dividend, have been greatly misrepresented, or misunderstood: And therefore praying, That the Petitioners may have Leave to lay before the House the true State of those Matters, and may be heard by themselves, or their Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as may affect their Interefi.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for further regulating the making of Dividends, by the United Company of Merchants of England, trading to the East Indies,is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard by their Counsel, before Vat. 3t.

Setting forth. That, in consequence of an Act, passed in the Fifth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for divesting the Petitioners of Senegal, and its Dependencies, there was no further Supply granted to them for Support of the Settlements at the said Place, after the 19th of October 1765, when it was expected His Majesty’s Troops would have taken Possession of the fame; and that the said Troops not arriving at Senegal till the 15th of April 1766, the Garrison established by the Petitioners were continued in Employment till the 29th <v

A Petition of the United Company of Merchants of England, trading to the Raft Indies,was presented to the

Vol. 31.

377

House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, being duly lenlible of the great Obligation they lie under to Government, and that their Interests are, and mull ever be, inseparable from those of the State, are moll earnellly desirous that the Public, and the East It* dia Company, should mutually reap the Benefits arising from the Acquifttions and Revenues lately obtained iu India; and the Petitioners conceiving, that in the present State of Things, a temporary Agreement for the Space of Three Years may be conducive to the Advantage of both, do submitto the Consideration of Parliament the following Propositions, in order to the carrying such Agreement into Execution: First. They beg Leave humbly to fuggcli, that it will be not only expedient, but necessary to the extending their Commerce, and enabling them to invest those Revenues in India in the Produce of the Country, that this House will take under their Consideration the Inland Duties upon Teas, in order to prevent the pernicious Practice of Smuggling, and encourage the Consumption of that Commodity by such an Alteration in the Duties as to the House shall seem fitting, and by granting a Drawback on such Teas as may be exported to Ireland, or to any of His Majesty’s Colonies, and also by such Alterations as may conduce to the same salutary Purposes, in regard to the Duties on Callicoes, Mullins, and raw Silk: Second. That in order to render the Advantages expectapt from the Revenues before mentioned certain and permanent^ the House will provide effectual Methods, as well for recruiting the Forces necessary in India, as for the regulating the Company’s Civil and Military Servants there, for preventing the Exportation of MilitaryStores thither except for the Company’s Service, and for preventing illicit Trade: Third. That from the said Revenues there shall be deducted the Expences attending the Collection thereof, together with the Civil, Military, and Marine Establishments, and also the Charges incurred for Fortifications, Buildings, and Repairs, the same to be adjusted by Annual Accounts transmitted from, and properly authenticated by, the several Presidencies in which the same shall be incurred: Fourth. That an Account of the Commerce of the Company, including the Residue of the said Revenues, and the Produce of their Exports, shall be Annually made up, and that out of the Sums arising from the General Sales, the Sum of £. 400,000 shall be deducted, in lieu of Profits which the Petitioners have hitherto enjoyed: Fifth. That the net Surplus shall be equally divided between the Public and the Company: Sixth. That the Company’s Share of the said Surplus shall be duly and solely appropriated to the Payment of their present Debts, until they ill all be reduced to the Sum due to the Company from the Public: Seventh. That this Agreement shall commence from the ill of February 1767, upon all Goods to be imported from India, and shall continue for Three Years, provided the Dewanne of Bengal, Bahar, and Orixa, shall remain in the Company’s Hands: Eighth. But if it should be the Opinion of the House, that it will be more beneficial for the Public to enjoy a specific Sum, instead of the Proportion of the Revenues and Trade above-mentioned, then the Petitioners propose to pay in lieu thereof, Four hundred thousand Pounds per Annum for Three Years, by Half-Yearly Payments; the First Payment thereof to commence the 25th of March 1768; and the}' are also willing to indemnify the Public in respect of such Drawback on Teas exported, as shall be thought fit to be granted by Parliament, taking the same on a Medium of the Duties on the Quantity of Teas exported for Five Years past; and that such Indemnification shall also extend to the Inland Duty of One Shilling in the Pound on the Quantities of all Black and Singlo Teas consumed in Britain, upon a

like Medium of Five Years, in case it shall also appear a fit Measure to Parliament to take off the said Duty; and, provided the Duties on the inereased Consumpt ion shall not be sufficient to replace or supp! v the aforesaid

5 D / Duty

Duty of One Shilling in the Pound; and the Petitioners hope, that what is hereby proposed, either in the Mode of Participation, or by a certain Yearly Payment, will appear reasonable and equitable to this House, more especially considering that the public Revenue,during this Interval, mult continually increase, in the same Proportion with the Commerce of the Company; and the Petitioners entreat the House to recollect the imminent Dangers to which, in many critical Conjunctures, their Property has been often exposed, the very large Sums they have expended since the Commencement of the Wars in India, in which they were never the Aggrelfors,

the low Dividends, which, notwithstanding their few Losses at Sea, thay have received, during a Course of Years, whilll the Public remained in the uninterrupted Perception of an Annual Revenue, arising from the Company’s Trade, of the full Value of One Third of their Capital, Circumstances, which, the Proprietors flatter themselves, will procure them the Favour and Protection of this Honourable House, and entitle them to that Candour and Justice which have ever been the Charac-teriftics of the British Senate.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to inquire further into the State and Condition of the East India Company.

A Petition of the several Persons, Inhabitants, or otherwise occasionally resident in the City of Bath, whose Names are thereunder subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are informed, a Bill is depending, for amending and explaining certain Laws relating to the Revenues of the Post Office, by which, the Petitioners are informed, the Post Matters are to be freed from the Duty of delivering of Letters at the Houses of the Persons to whom they are directed, which, if the same lliould pass into a Law, would subject the Petitioners, and many others of His Majesty’s Subjects, to many and great Inconveniences: And therefore praying, that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, or so much thereof as relates to the Delivery of Letters, or may otherwise affect their Interests, or that the House will grant them such other Relief in the Premises as shall seem meet.

AClause was offered to be added to the Bill, allowing a greater Number of Votes toPersons possessed of more than £. 500 Stock.

And the said Clause was, with Leave of the House, withdrawn.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, that noPerson to whom Stock shall be transferred, after a certain Day, shall have a Right to vote till he shall have been in Possession a certain Time.

And the said Clause was Twice read, with Blanks; which being filled up, the said Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, that no Person shall be capable of being a Director till he has been in Possession of his Qualification a certain Time.

And the said Clause was Once read, with Blanks; and, with Leave of the House, withdrawn.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

After which, His Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from tjio ThoRe, to both Houses of Parliament; as followethj viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The King’s The advanced Season of the Year, joined to the Con-' Speech. Adoration of the Inconvenience you ipuft all have felt from so long an Absence from your feyqral Counties, calls upon Me to put an End to the present Session of Parliament, which I cannot do, without returning you My Thanks for your diligent Application to the Publip Business, and the Proofs you have given of your Affection for Me, for My Family, and for My Government: And although, from the Nature and Extefoiveness gf

12

the several Objects under yottr Consideratiott, it could not be expected, that all the great commercial Interests should be completely adjusted and regulated in the Course of this Session, yet I am persuaded, that by the Progressyou have made, a solid Foundation is laid for securing the most considerable and essential Benefits to this.Nation.

As no material Alteration has happened in the State of foreign Affairs since your First Meeting, I have nothing to communicate to you on that Subject. The fixed Objects of all My Measures are to preserve the Peace, and at the same Time, to assert and maintain the Honour of My Crown, and the just Rights of My People.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I thank you for the necessary Supplies which you have so cheerfully granted for the Public Service; and My particular Acknowledgements are due to you, for the Provision you have enabled Me to make for the more honourable Support and Maintenance of My Family.'

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The great Attention which you have shewn to the particular Purpose for which I called you so early together, and the very wholesome Laws polled for relieving My Subjects from the immediate Distress which the great Scarcity of Corn threatened to bring upon them, give Me the most fcniible Pleasure. I rely upon you for the Exertion of your utmost Endeavours to convince My People, that no Care has been wanting to procure for them every Relief which has been possible; and that their grateful Sense of Provisions so wifely made for their present Happiuefs and lasting Prosperity cannot be so fully expressed, as by a strict Observance of that Order and Regularity, which are equally necessary to the Security of all good Government, as well as to their owa real Welfare.

After which the Lord Chancellor, by His Majesty’s Command, said:

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is His Majesty’s Royal Will and Pleasure, That this Parliafl&'j Parliament be prorogued to Monday the Thirty-first prorajui Day of Augajl next, to be then here held: And this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Monday the Thirty-first Day of August next.

A Bill for the more effectual preventing clandeiline Outlawries, was read the First Time.

Mr. Speaker reported, that the House had attended His Majesty in the House of Peers; where His Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which Mr. Speaker said he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have chosen to call you together at this Season of the Year, that My Parliament might have fullTime for their Deliberations upon all such Branches of the Public Service as may require their immediate Attention; without the Necessity of continuing the Section beyond the Time moil suitable to My People for the Election of a new Parliament: And I doubt not but you will be careful, from the said Considerations, to avqid in your Proceedings all unnecessary Delay.

Nothing in the present Situation of Affairs Abroad givesMeReal’on to apprehend, that you will be prevent-

Vol.V*

ed,by any Interruption of the Public Tranquillity, from fixing your whole Attention upon such Points as concern the internal Welfare and Prosperity of My People.

Among these Objects of adomeftic Nature, none can demand a more speedy or more serious Attention, than what regards the high Price of Corn; which neither the

ialutary Laws paired in the last Session of Parliament,' nor the Produce of the late Harvest, have yet been able so far to reduce, as to give sufficient Relief to the Dif-tresses of the poorer Sort of My People. Your late Residence in your several Countries mult have enabled you to judge whether any further Provision can be made, conducive to the Attainment of so delirable an bind.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I will order the proper Officers to lay before you the Estimates for the Service of the ensuing Year.

The Experience I have had of your constant Readi-ness to grant Me all such Supplies as should be found necessary for the Security, Interest, and Honour of the Nation (and I have no other to ask of you) renders it unnecessary for Me to add any Exhortations upon this Head: And I doubt not but the same Public Confi-' derations will induce you to persevere, with equal Alacrity, in your Endeavours to diminish the National Debt; while, on My Part, no Care shall be wanting to contribute, as far as possible, to the Attainment of that most eftential Object, by every frugal Application of such Supplies as you shall grant.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Necessity of improving the present general Tranquillity to the great Purpose of maintaining the Strength the Reputation, and the Prosperity of this Country, ought to be ever before your Eyes. To render your Deliberations for that Purpose successful, endeavour to cultivate a Spirit of Harmony among yourselves. My Concurrence in whatever will promote the Happiness of My People you may always depend upon: And in that Light I shall ever be deftrous of encouraging Union among all those who with well to their Country.

Fifthly, That the present Regulations in the Assize of Bread fcem highly disadvantageous to the Poor, who, as the Petitioners humbly conceive, might be supplied cheaper, and better, if only one Sort of Bread was made assize-able. Sixthly, That the great Increase in the Breed of Horses (owing partly to the growing Practice of em-( ploying them, instead of Oxen, in Tillage, and partly to the great Demands from Abroad), has greatly contributed to diminish the Number of Cattle for Slaughter, and necessarily tends to enhance the Price thereof, which, the Petitioners apprehend, might be corrected, by a Duty upon the Exportation of Horses, and a small Bounty upon Jthe Use of Oxen in Tillage. Seventhly,

That the Scarcity of grownCattle, and consequently the

Deamefs of Flelli Meat, are still further increased by the unlimited Destruction of Ewe Lambs, and Cow-Calves, in all Seasons of the Year, merely to gratify the unreasonable Appetite of the Rich and Luxurious. Eighthly, That the prevailing Practice of consolidating small farms not only tends to render many Articles of Provision and Consumption scarce, but must, in Time, depopulate the Country of its moil useful Inhabitants, by depriving the industrious Poor both of Labour and Habitation. Lastly, that the misguided and often ill-grounded Resentment of the common People, in Times of Public Calamity (by prompting them to destroy Mills, Com, and other Provisions, and to obstruct the Removal of the latter from one Place to another), is not only an Injury to their Fellow Subjects, but also to themselves, by aggravating the very Evils they complain of; and therefore, for their Sakes, as well as that of the Public, ought to be timely and effectually prevented, or suppressed: And therefore praying the House, to take these important Matters into their moil serious Consideration, and to provide such Remedies as their respective Natures shall appear to require, or admit; and such as the House shall judge confident with the real and permanent Interests of the whole Kingdom.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right usual to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to Orden. serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House, will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the faipe is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House w ill proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before this House, or. any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Resolved, That in all Cases of controverted Elections for Counties in England and Wales, to be heard at the Bar of this House, or before the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Petitioners do, by themselves or by their Agents, within a convenient Time, to be appointed either by the House, or the Committee of Privileges and Elections, as the Matter to be heard shall be before the House or the said Committee,deliver to the Sitting Members or their Agents, Lifts of the Persons intended by the Petitioners to be objected to, who voted for the Sitting Members; giving, in the said Lifts, the several Heads of Objection, and distinguishing the same against the Names of the Voters excepted to; and that the Sitting Members do, by themselves or by their Agents, within the same Time, deliver the like Lifts, on their Part to the Petitioners or their Agents.

Answer Mr. Speaker reported to the House, that the House Address attended His Majesty Yesterday, with their Address; to which His Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer:

Gentlemen,

I return you My very fincereThanks for your dutiful and loyal Address; the Part you take in the late happy Event in My Family completes the Satisfaction which I receive from it; and your Affection to Me appears equally manifest, from the Share you take in the melancholy Incident which we all regret, and serves as a Consolation to Me. I fee with Pleasure the Continuance of that Zeal, and true public Spirit, which I have long experienced in My faithful Commons, by your Attention to the several Objects recommended to your Consideration, and particularly to the Means of providing against a Scarcity of Corn, and for paying the Public Debt. You may depend upon My invariable Attention to the Happiness and Prosperity of My Kingdom.

Ditto. A Petition offeveral Merchants, and Maltsters, having Stocks of Malt, made for Exportation between the 1 -jth November 1 766, and the Palling of thelaft Act Jorprohibiting the Exportation of Corn, Malt,tfc. was 11

presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That in the Act of the Sixth of His present Majesty, prohibiting the Exportation of Corn, Malt, 8Cc. Liberty was given to export such Malt as had been made or wetted for Exportation before the Day the Act received the Royal Assent; and that the Petitioners, apprehending that the same Indulgence would be given in the lateA6t, for prohibiting the Exportation of Corn, Malt, continued in their usual Course of Business to make Malt, SCc. for Exportation, till that Act received the Royal Assent, which was in December or January last; but the Petitioners found, to their Surprize, that the Act con* fined the Liberty of exporting Malt to what was made for Exportation, and to Barley that wasfieeped, on or before the 15th November, and that the Petitioners thei\ waited the Expiration of the Act, in Expectation of

being at Liberty to export their Malt, after the iothDay of September; but, by the Proclamation lately ill’ued, the same Prohibition is continued, and the Malt llill remains locked up in the King’s Store-rooms under the King’s Locks; and that the said Malt is only, fit for the Dutch Distillers, being made from Barley of'an inferior Quality, and not fit to make Malt for Home Coniump-tion, and will be certainly spoiled, and probably eaten up by Vermin, unless they, can be permitted to export it; and therefore hope, that when the above Circumstances shall be duly cohfidered,' they shall meet with such Indulgence as their same may appear to merit, and not be injured in their Property by an Act which undoubtedly is of the greatest Benefit to the Nation in general, and will not be less so if the Petitioners are allowed to export their Malt, for which they hope to obtain Leave by aClause in the next Prohibition Bill for prohibiting the Exportation of Corn, as their Quantity is too l’mall to answer the Expence of a private Act.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Twenty-ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for regulating, the Nightly Watch and Beadles, and cleansing, enlightening, and paving the Streets, Squares, Lanes, and other Passages, and repairing the Highways and Causeways, and regulating the Poor, within the Parilli of Saint Mary le Bone, in the County of Middlesex, was read:

And Mr. William Guthrey said, That the Act has been found in several Respects ineffectual to answer the Purposes thereby intended, particularly in the Appointment of Parish Officers.

And the Witness mentioned several Instances of Persons, who before they had been Two Years out of Office as O verfeer, and feme as soon as out of that Office, were appointed Constables, which he thinks a great Abuse of Power; and cannot be remedied by the present Law.

ampfoti, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, by an Act passed in the Twenty-second Year of King George the Second, for repairing and widening the Road from Kingston upon Thames, in the County of Surrey, to Sheet Bridge, near Petersfleld, in the County of Southampton; and also, the Road from Hindhead Heath, through Femluir(l Lane and Midhurst, to the City of Chichester, several Tolls and Powers were granted to certain Trustees therein named, for repairing the first* mentioned Road, from Kingston upon Thames to Sheet Bridge,and that, in pursuance of such Powers, the said Trustees for the said Branch, have proceeded in the Repairs of the said Road, and have borrowed a considerable sum of Money upon the Credit of the said Tolls, and a large Debt still remains thereupon; and that it will be impossible to keep the said Road in Repair, and pay off the Debt, during the subsistingTerm; and that the said Act has, in several other Parts, been found defective; and that an Act passed in the Thirty-third Year of King George the Second, for extending the Navigation of the River Wey, from Guildford to Godalming, which has since been completed, at a large Expence, and hath been very beneficial to the said Counties; but, from the Effect of some late Measures, the Intent of the said Act seems likely to be defeated; and that the Petitioners beg Leave further to represent, that the said Branch of Road, from Kingston upon Thames to Sheet Bridge, is morg than Forty Miles long, and the Meetings of the Trustees, usually held at Eflier,

or Guildford, all which Places are in the Northern Division of the said Road, and are from Twenty-three to Thirty-six Miles distant from the Southern Extremity of the fame, which makes it impossible for the Trustees residing the re to attend those Meetings without a manifest Inconvenience and Prejudice to their private Affairs; and the Number of such Trustees are small, compared with those who reside on or near the Northern Parts of the said Road, the Trustees residing in the Town of Guildford, and that Part oiStoke immediatelyadjoining thereto (where the Meetings are usually held), being Thirty in Number, very near One Fifth of the Whole, which Inequality prevents the Operation of the said Acts in their full Extent, and confines what the Legislature intended for a public Advantage, only to a local One:

And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to

bring in a Bill to enlarge the Term and Powers granted

by the said Act of the Twenty-second Year of his late

Majesty’s Reign, so far as relates to the said Branch of

Road, from Kingston upon Thames, in the County of

Surrey, to Sheet Bridge, near Peterffie in the County of Southampton; and for dividing the said Roads into

Two Districts, under separateTrufts.

Mr. Paterson, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four hundred and Sixteen thousand Four hundred and Three Pounds and Eleven Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for the Ordinary of the Navy, including Half Pay to Sea and Marine Officers, for the Year 1768.

Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Number of Land Forces, including Two thousand Four hundred and Sixty Invalids, amounting to Seventeen thousand Two hundred and Fifty-three effective Men, Commission and Non-Commission Officers included, be employed for the Year 1768.

Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six hundred and Six thousand Two hundred and Twenty-one Pounds Twelve Shillings and Ten Pence and Seven-Eighths of a Penny, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Seventeen thousand Two hundred and Fifty-three effective Men, for Guards, Garrisons, and other His Majesty’s Land Forces, in Great Britain, Guernsey, and Jersey, for the Yrear 1768.

Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Three hundred Ninety-six thousand Nine hundred and Fifty Pounds Four Shillings and Nine Pence and Seven-Eighths of a Penny, be granted to His Majesty, for maintaining His Majesty’s Forces and Garrisons in the Plantations and Africa, including those in Garrison at Minorca and Gibraltar, and for Provisions for the Forces in North America, Nova Scotia, Netvfomdland, Gibraltar, the ceded Islands, and Africa, for the Year 1768.

Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Seven thousand Two hundred and Twenty-six Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Two Pence Halfpenny, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of the Ditference of Pay between the Britishand Irish Establishment of Six Regiments of

Foot, serving in the Ijle of Man, at Minorca,

and the ceded Islands, for the Year 1768.

*7

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Twelve thousand Two hundred and Thirty-seven Pounds Seven Shillings and Three Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for the Pay of the General and General Staff Officers in Great Britain, for the Year 1768.

Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Five thousand Two hundred and Twenty-seven Pounds Fourteen Shillings, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Full Pay, for Three hundred and Sixty-six Days, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-eight, to Officers reduced, with the Tenth Company of several Battalions reduced from Ten to Nine Companies, and who remained on Half Pay at the 24th Day of December 1765.

Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred Fifty-nine thousand Three hundred and Twenty-eight Pounds Eleven Shillings and Sixpence, be granted to His Majesty, for the Charge of the Office of Ordnance, for Land Service, for the Year 1768.

Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Sixty-eight thousand Nine hundred and Forty-four Pounds Twelve Shillings and Eleven Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Expence of Services performed by the Office of Ordnance, for Land Service, and not provided for by Parliament in 1767.
