A Petition of several Merchants, and Maltders, hav-0 ing Stocks of Malt made for Exportation between the

15th November 1766, and the passing of the Act lad Year for prohibiting the Exportation of Corn, Malt, Sc. was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That in the Act of the Sixth of His present Ma-x jedy, prohibiting the Exportation of Corn, Malt, Sc. Liberty was given to export such Malt as had been made or wetted for Exportation before the Day the Act received the Royal Assent; and that the Petitioners, apprehending the same Indulgence would be given in the Act of lad Year, for prohibiting the Exportation of Corn, Malt, Sc. continued in their usual Course of Business, to make Malt for Exportation, till that Act received the Royal Assent, which was the 16th Day of December lad; but the Petitioners found, to their Surprize, that the Act confined the Liberty of exporting Malt to what was made for Exportation, and to Barley that was steeped, on or before the 15th 17 66;

and that the Petitioners then waited the Expiration of the Act, in Expectation of being at Liberty to export ' their Malt, but, by the Act lately passed, the Prohibition is continued, and the Malt, dill remains locked up in the King’s Store-Rooms, under the King’s Locks; and that the said Malt is only fit for the Dutch Distilleries, being made from Barley of an inferior Quality, and not from Barley fit to make Malt for Home Consumption, and will be certainly spoiled, and probably eaten up by the Vermin, unless they can be permitted to export it; and that the Petitioners therefore hope, when the above Circumstances shall be duly considered, they shall meet with such Indulgence as their same may appear to merit, and not to be injured in their Property by an Act which undoubtedly is of the greated Benefit to the Nation in general, and will not be less so if the Petitioners be allowed to export their Malt: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for permitting the Petitioners to export the said Malt, or that the House will give the Petitioners such other Relief as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine, and date to the House, the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition:

An Account of the Quantity of Wheat, and Wheat-flour, and other Species of Grain and Pulse, imported into England, from any Part of Europe or Africa, from 5th Day of January 1767 to the 10th of October following, which is as far as the same can be made up; distinguishing the several Places from whence the same were imported: And also.

The House resolved itself into a Conimitteeof the Salted whole House, upon the Bill to continue and amend an PrOTlfion Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act for Importation of salted Beef, Pork, Bacon, and Butter, from Ireland, for a limited Time.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, William Guthry, Esquire, said, That there is an Hospital in Quebec Street, in the said Parish, called The General Lying-in Hojpilal, which was formerly in George's Parish, but since transferred to Maryle Bwhich Hospital has no Charter, but supported only by voluntary Subscriptions.

That upon a Medium of Four Years past, 40 Children have been annually born in the said Hospital, which Children become burthensome to the Parish, and mult be the Ruin of the Parish, if not speedily remedied; and that as the Buildings in the said Parish increase, the Grievance is the greater.

Mr. Geo. Rawlinjon, being examined, confirmed the above Evidence.

Mr. Abbot Newell Cockman, Vestry Clerk of the said Parish, produced the Vestry Books for Years past,whereby it appeared, that 79 Women had been delivered in the said Hospital within that Period, which have become chargeable to the Parish.

And Mr. Guthry, being asked the Question, he said, That any Hospital within the said Parish, for the general Reception of Lying-in Women, would be attended with great Inconvenience.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Jerome Knapp, Esquire, Clerk of the Assize for the Home Circuit, being examined, said. That the present Shire House of the County of Hertford, is extremely small and inconvenient: That the Court on the Crown Side is very bad; and that on the Nisi Prius Side so cold, that the Judges cannot fit there in the Lent Circuit.

Mr. John Hall, Under Sheriff of the County of Hertford, confirmed Mr. Knapp's Evidence.

Mr. James Adams, Architect, being examined, said.

That the present Shire House is an ancient Building, very ruinous and incommodious: and it is necessary that the same should be taken down and rebuilt.

Mr. William llanfcombe Carpenter, being examined,

confirmed Mr. Adams's Evidence:

And Mr. Adams added. That if certain Messuages,

Sheds or Shambles, now Handing near the present Shire House were taken down, a commodious Shire House may be built there.

Sir Robert Ladbroke reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being a Committee appointed by the whole Body of Master Taylors residing within the City of London, and some Miles round the fame, in behalf of themselves and the rest of the said Body, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition j and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his

Vol. 31.

Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the Seventh Year of the Reign of King George the First, for regulating the Journeymen Taylors within the wreekly Bills Of Mortality, was read, whereby it appeared, that Prosecutions for Offences were to be commenced within Six Days after the Offence committed, and all Prosecutions to be heard before the Session. And,

Mr. John Morgan, being examined, said, That he had applied to Five Justices at one and the same Time, on Complaint against the Master Taylors for not complying with the Act; and, upon examining into the Act* they unanimously relolved that the Act was insufficient so as to give Relief; and refused to act under it; and that the Witness had made several Applications of the same nature, but could get no Relief.

Mr. William Davis and Mr. Thomas Racket, being severally examined, said, That several Master Taylors have evaded the Act by taking Houses at Mary It Bone and other Places out of the Bills of Mortality, out of the Limits prescribed by the Act.

And both the said Witnesses further said. That they have, in Conversation, heard Mailer Taylors say, that they have carried their Work and Workmen out of the Bills of Mortality, by which Means neither the Justices nor the King’s Bench could touch them; by that Means they give larger Wages, and, in Times of hurry, can get Journeymen from other Matters, which gives those Masters Advantage in Trade, and have gotCustomers from them: And that the Act is insufficient to prevent the above Grievances, and in several other Respects inefl’eftual to answer the Purposes thereby intended.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to amend an Act, made in the Seventh Y’ear of King George the First, intituled, An Act for regulating the Journeymen Taylors within the weekly Bills of Mortality: And that Sir Robert Ladbroke and Mr. Upton do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of several Merchants, His Majesty’s British Vol. 31.

Subjects, concerned in the Whale Fishery, on behalf of themselves and others concerned in the said Fishery, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth.

That by an Act of Parliament, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His Majesty King George the First, a Bounty was granted of Twenty Shillings a Ton upon all Ships employed in catching of Whales in the Green-laitd and Seas adjacent: but few or no Ships being fitted out upon that Encouragement, a further Bounty of Ten Shillings a Ton was granted by an Act of the Thirteenth Year of his late Majesty’s Reign; and that being also found insufficient to answer the Purposes intended, the Bounty was, by an Act of the Twenty-second Year of his said late Majesty, increased to Forty Shillings per Ton, and which, by Two several Acts, have been continued to the 25th of December 1767*

6 X

East India Company’s

Dividends.

v%

22° — cl50 Januarii.

A. 1768.

and to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and that, since the granting of that Bounty, a great many Ships from both Parts of the United Kingdom have been annually employed in the said Fishery, and many more would have adventured, but from the Checks given to that Trade, first by the War,-and afterwards by the Shortness of the Time granted for the Bounty by the last Act; and that, if rrovision was made to continue the Bounty for a further Term of Seven Years, it would considerably increase the Number of Adventurers, by which Means a Nursery for the hardiest Race of Seamen would beestablished, and several of our Manufacturers, who have been already instructed in the making the proper Utensils and Instruments employed in this Fishery, would be constantly engaged therein $ and that, if the Bounty is not further continued, the Trade mull be entirely at a Stand, the Charge of fortifying*^ Ship against the Ice for that Service, and the Fishing Materials, which are the greatest Part of the Expence, being entirely useless for any other Business; and that the Petitioners humbly presume an Object of such great national Importance will be deemed deferring the Continuance of the Support and Encouragement of the Legislature: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the Petition of the Merchants and Tradesmen of the Port of Liver* pool, on behalf of themselves, and more particularly of those concerned in the Whale Fishery to Greenland, Davis's Straits, and the Seas adjacent, is referred.

Mr. Fuller, according to Order, reported from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Complaint made to the House upon the First Day of December last, that, in Breach of the Privilege of this House, Henry Fidler, John Baker, and Matt here Barrozv, had, by the Instiga-tion of Charles Boziycr Adderley, Esquire, forcibly entered upon a Fishery at Coton, on the River Tame, the Property of, and in the Possession of, Simon Luttrell, Esquire, a Member of this House, and taken Fish thereout; together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read: and is as followeth; viz.

The Counsel for the Member making the Complaint in order to prove that an exclusive Fishery on the River Tame, between Coton Bridge and an Eate, called The Lord's Eate, to have been a considerable Time in the

Possession of the said Member, and of the Family of the Cotons, from whence the Estate at Coton derived to him, called the following Witnesses; viz.

Sir Robert Lawley, Baronet; who said, he was conversant with the Family of the Cotons near Sixty Years; That they had a considerable Estate on the Banks of the River Tame, near the Fishery in Question; and that the Member making the Complaint married the Representative of that Family, and came into the Estate about 1733: That the Witness about 28 Years ago, rented the Fishery in Question, viz. between Coton Bridge and the Lord's Eate, and held it about Six Years; during which Timeit was an entire and exclusive Fishery belonging to the Coton Family: That there was no Interruption from any one claiming a Right: That during his whole Know- ledge of the said Fishery, which has been near Thirty Years, he never heard that any Person fished it except those employed by Mr. Luttrell the Member: That he has heard, that Mr. Adderley, named in the Complaint, and Mr. Dilkes, have ajoint Fishery in other Parts of the River Tame, but never heard till lately, that Mr. Adder ley claimed the Fishery in Question: That Mr. Churchill succeeded the Witness in the Fishery, who held it about Ten Years, and died about Six Months ago.

Upon being cross examined, the Witness said. That he paid Twenty Shilling or a Guinea a Year for the Fishery: That his House is Four computed Miles from the River, but could say, that no one fished there to his Knowledge: That he rented the Fishery Twice, First for Five or Six Years, then a second Time of Mr. Churchill above-mentioned, for Three or Four Years; and that he fished Five or Six Times under both those Holdings.

Andrew Hackett, Esquire, a Gentleman of W'artoick-shire, who said he succeeded Mr. Churchill, and rented the Fishery in question of the Member, from 1757 to 1761; that he rented it as an exclusive Fishery, and was never interrupted: That he has known it Thirty Years, and never knew any Right claimed by Mr. Adderley, Mr. Dilkes, or any one.

Being cross examined, he said, he had no Leaie; that he took it of Mr. Luttrells Steward as Coton Fishery; made no Bargain, but took it as it was: That his Residence is about a Mile and Half from the River: That the Limits of the Fishery were not described to him; That he does not know of Mr. Adderley's using the Fishery when he had it; that he never met with any Interruption, if he had, he should have applied to his Landlord, not knowing the Bounds himself; that he gave Twenty Shillings a Year for it, till Mr. Luttrell sent him Word, he desired to have it in his own Hands: That he never heard of any one’s fishing the re, but with an Angle: That Mr. Dilkes was Lord of the Manor of Mackjlock during the Time he had the Fishery: That he has heard he has a Right, but does not know it: That Coton and Marston are within the Manor of Mack-fiock; and the Fishery he rented is within Coton; that he did not consider it as exclusive: He took it as Mr. Luttrells Fishery; was not absolutely certain whether it was exclusive; That he did not know the Right of the Lord of the Manor of Mackjlock, as to the Fishery in Question: That John Starkie had the Care of it for him, and fished it frequently with Calling Nets, Hooks, and Lines, and otherwise; if any one else had so fished, he should have complained to the Steward: And being again asked the Question, he said. That when he took it he underilood it to be exclusive; and that he never heard of any one’s claiming to fish, but Mr. Luttrell.

Mr. Thomas Fulhooood, a Farmer, who said, he had rented and lived at Coton Hall the last Thirty Years, till last Lady Day; and that he rented it of Mr, Luttrell; that the Hall is about Twenty Yards from the River: That the Fishery in Question belongs to Mr. Luttrell; that he never knew any one, but him and his Tenants, fish there, nor ever heard of any other Claim, or of any Dispute relating to it till now.

Being cross examined, he (bid, he never knew of any

Sarah Kenrick, Daughter of the last Witness, who said, the had lived with her Father at Coton Hall, and never heard of Mr. Adderley and Mr. Dilkes using the Fishery in question.

John Starkie said, he was Servant to the aforesaid Mr. Hacketty during the time he rented the Fishery in Question, and frequently fished; that he never knew any one else claim it: That he was informed of the Boundary of the Fishery by Fidler, one of the Persons complained of, who called lit his Purlieu, and that he took care of it for Mr. Luttrell; and the Witness said, he never knew any public Fishing by Mr. Adderley or any one else: That there are joint Rights of Fishing above the Bridge and below the Eate.

Being cross examined, he said, he could not tell who fished, for he was in the Garden the greatest Part of his Time: That Fidler shewed them where to fish: That he had heard Mr. Palmer, the Steward of Mr. Luttrell say, it was Mr. Luttrell's exclusive Right; and that it was in general understood so by all the Country.

Mr. John Hackett said, he had lived at Coton all his Life: That the Fishery in Question was always reckoned Mr. Luttrell's ,* that he has fished there several Times with Fidler for Mr. Luttrell, and never knew any one else fish within those Limits: That he has known Fidler fish in other Parts for Mr. Adderley; and that Fidler has told him that Mr. Luttrell*s Fishery begun at the Bridge: That he never knew Mr. Adderley, nor any one for him, fish there till this Dispute.

Mr. John Mills said, he lives Fifty Yards from the River: That the Fishery in Question was always reckoned Mr. Luttrell's own Right, and that he never heard of any Pretenfton being made to it; but that it is the general Sense, that Mr. Adderley has a joint Right with Mr. Luttrelly One hundred and fifty Yards above the Bridge, and about One hundred below the Eate, to the Spiral Mead.

Then, to prove the actual fishing by the Persons complained of, the said Counsel called,

Jc %res Allen, who said. That he knows Henry Fidler, John Bakery and Mattheio Barroivy the Persons complained of; that he saw them fishing at a place called Black Pool, between Coton Bridge, and the Lord's Eate; that he went to them, and said to Fidler, " I thought

Mr. Palmer had discharged you from fishing here," whereupon they skulked away, but afterwards came forward again, and drew their Net: That Mr. Luttrell came to the Place soon after, and asked the said Baker if he did not know it to be his Fishery, who said he knew it was, and begged his Pardon, saying, he was employed by Mr. Adderley to do it: That the others ran away with the Nets; and that the said Fidler had lliewn the witness Mr. Luttrell's Fishery.

Being cross examined, he said Baker was a Tenant to Mr. Luttrell, but did not think what he said when Mr. Luttrell came up was on that Account: That he is very bold, but asked Pardon several Times.

Then the Counsel for the Parties named in the Complaint, in order to prove the Exercife of the Fishery in question by Mr. Dilkes and Mr. Adderley, called the following Witnesses; viz.

Mr. Mark Love, who said, he has known the Fishery fh question 45 Years, and wTas a Tenant to Mr. Dilkes 45 Years ago: That he has gone with the Keeper and others, and fished all through, between the Bridge and the Eate, arid further down, and that Part between the Bridge and the Eate without Distinction: That he did so Twenty Times at the least, and never met with any Interruption, nor ever heard Mr. Dilkes's Right called in question; and that it was generally understood to be his Right.

Being cross examined, he said, he fished every where without Interruption; that he has known nothing of it for

Yol. 31.

the last 2 z Years: That they sometimes fished till Three in the Afternoon.

Francis Holyoak said, he has been employed to fish Privilege, by the late Mr. Dilkes, all the Way from the Bottom to the Hall; that they always fished publicly, and never were interrupted: That they generally fished Once a Year, but fomfcimes miffed a Year: That they used to convey their Nets there in a Tumbril drawn by Three Horses: and that they might be seen from the Hall when they were fishing.

Being cross examined, and asked if he ever saw Mr.

Coton or Mr. Luttrell fish there, he said he did not know who fished there at other Times, nor ever knew that any one but Mr. Dilkes and Mr. Adderley had any Right there: That the last Time he fished was 22 Years ago; and he knows nothing of it since.

James Brookes said, the Lord of the Manor was reported to have a Fishery through the wholq River; and that he had heard Thomas Coton, Esquire, say so: That a Person asking Mr. Coton's Leave to angle in Coton 1 Water, he said, he would give him Leave, as far as he could; that this Conversation happened above 50 Years ago.

Mr. Robert Morris said, he has known the Fishery in question upwards of 50 Years: That the Lord of the Manor and his Servants fished in all Parts of the River, but that the last he remembers of it was 50 Years ago; and that during his Time they were never disturbed.

Mr. John Kijs said, he was employed to fish in the Part in question with Mrs. Adderley's Game Keeper 13 Years ago: That they fished a pretty many Times, but never met with any Interruption: That the Reputation was, that Mr. Adderley has a Right to fish in the Parts in question.

Being cross examined, he said, he fished in the deep Draught about Six Years ago, with a Net; that he cannot say whether he was seen by Mr. Luttrell or any of his Friends: That he fished 5 or 6 Years between the Bridge and the Eate: That neither Mr. Luttrell or his Servants fished there at the same Time, but that they have fished there; that the Witness did not forbid them, there being no Objection on any Side.

Richard Wright, Mr. Adderley's Game Keeper, said, he has fished in the Water in question lately: That he began Two Years ago and upwards, and fished all' through, from Coxe's Hall to Mawkees, which takes in from the Bridge at Coton to below the Lord's Eate: That he fished thereThree Times, and was never interrupted:

That Mr. Luttrell's Tenants have seen him fish, but never questioned him: That he never heard Mr. Luttrell had an exclusive Right, but that it was understood Mr. Adderley had as much Right as Mr. Luttrell

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Richard Whitby, being examined, said, That there is a Parcel of Land within the said Borough, called Nun's Green; and that, for some Years past, many Erections and Incroachments have been made thereon, and Gravel is dug for private and particular Uses, as well as for the Turnpike Roads, which makes Pits; wherein great Quantities of Water stagnate, and become offensive and detrimental to the Health of the Inhabitants of the said Borough.

That the Inhabitants of the said Borough are One Third more in Number than Twenty Years ago, and therefore in great Want of more Monies for their Iteli-dence; and that, if Power was given to fell some Part of the said Green, to build Houses thereon, and to prevent Encroachments and Nilifauces for the future, it would he of great Utility to all Persons haring a Right of Common on the said Green, and to all Persons residing in the said Borough j and that it would like wife be very advantageous if the Remainder of the said Green were made a Stinted Common.

Mr. William Merry Locket confirmed the above Evidence.

Ordered, That T-cave be given to bring in a Bill for felling Part of a Green, called Nun's Green, in the Borough of Derby, in the County of Derby, and for applying the Money arising from the Sale thereof, in the improvement of the remaining Part of the said Green, and for oilier Purposes therein mentioned: And that Mr. Filzherbert, Mr. Coutts, and Lord Frederick Cuvendish,do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

.1768.

Copy of a Letter from t he Mayor, &>. of the City of Oxford,to the Honourable Robert Lee, dated 1 )jai/ 170b.

S1 Oxford, 12th Map 1700.

rT'II E Debts and Circumfianees of the City'of

having been laid before a Council of the City, held by Order of the Mayor on Monday the 24th March last and it then appearing that the City were indebted to' their Bond Creditors in the Sum oi £. 5,670, exclusive of the Annuities, Benefactions, and Charities, which are paid by the City, and annually amount to more than the net Income of their Estates: And as some Person or Persons have, without the Consent of the Council of this City, taken upon themselves to expose the City to a Person in London, by offering to elect any Two Persons

to be Representatives for this City in Parliament at the next General Election, who would advance £.4,000: The Mayor and Council have therefore unanimously eome to a Resolution, in order to prevent all Opposition, Animolity, and Confusion, and to extricate tlicm-selves out of their present Difficulties, to apply to you and Sir Thomas Stapleton (in the first Instance) for your Assistance to discharge the Bond Debts due from the City, by which Means they will be enabled to do Justice to their Creditors, and, as they apprehend, preserve Peace and Unanimity in the City. But if it should not be agreeable to you and Sir Thomas to advance the Money, the whole Council are determined to apply to some other Person or Persons in the County to do it, and if possible, by that Means, to keep themselves from being sold to Foreigners. We therefore, whose Names are hereunder written, have, by Order of the Council, taken the Liberty of troubling you With the above, and also with the inclosed State of the City Debts and Income; and as we are directed by the Council to report your Answer to them, so we mull beg Leave to trouble you to fend your Answer to the Mayor as soon as it is agreeable to you, that he may call a Council, and lay the same before them.

We are. Sir,

Your most obedient humble Servants,

Phip Ward, Mayor,

John Treacher,

Tho*

Thot Wife,

John Nicholes,

John Phillips,

Isaac Lawrance,

Richd Tawney,

Anthony Weston,

In Brown, j

P. S. The Corporation think themselves very much obliged to you for your late generous Benefaction to them, and are sorry their Necefiities oblige them to trouble you with this Letter.

To the Honourable Robert

Copy of a Letter from the Honourable Robert Lee and Sir Thomas Stapleton, to the Mayor, fife, of Oxford, dated 30 July 1766.

Ordered, That the said Papers do remain in the Custody of the Clerk of this House; and that he do not deliver the same to any Person, without Order of this House.

Mr. Mayor, and Gentlemen,

TY7 E think it incumbent on us to return you Thanks ' ’ for the Preference you are generously pleased to give us of purchasingyour Corporation; but as we never intend to fell you, so we cannot afford the Purchase. As it has been always our determined Resolution, that if we could not serve our Country, we would not be concerned in betraying it; while you remained independent we thought it a peculiar Honour to represent you; and had you continued in that State we should have been heartily and sincerely at your Service.

Rob'

Stapleton.

of the County of Somerset, at a numerous Meeting, held at Yeovill,in the said County, the 8th Day of January 1763; and all’o, the Petition of the Gentlemen, Graziers, and others, Feeders of Cattle, in the County of Dorset, at a very numerous Meeting held at Sturminfer Newton CtijUe,in the said County, the Thirteenth Day of January x 7 68; and also, the Petition of the Justices of the Peace, assembled at their General Quarter Session for the County of Somerset, and of the Gentlemen of the Grand Inquest, and of other Gentlemen, Clergy, arul Freeholders of the said County; were severally referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Sir Abraham. Elton, Baronet, being examined, said, That he acts as a Ji’tMce of the Peace for the County of Somerset: That he has had frequent Complaints from Graziers of the illegal Practices made use of by Jobbers of Cattle, but could give no Remedy, as the Law requires Two M Unifies to prove the Offence, which isalmost impossible to he procured, as the Trans-action is only between the Buyer and Seller:

That the Justices at the General Quarter Sessions complain of this Grievance, and of the Impracticability of bringing Offenders to Juliiceas the Law now Hands; and that he thinks the only effectual Check to the illegal Jobbing of Cattle would be, that any One J office should have a Power, where there is a sufficient Cause to suspect a Breach of the Law, to bind the sup-pofedOffenders to the Sessions, where the Onus should lie upon the Person accused: That if this Practice w as suppressed, it would be beneficial to the Counties near London, as the frequent shifting of Cattle, from

Hand to 1 land, for Half a Crown Profit, is the reason they are never fed properly.

Upon the whole Matter, your Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolvei i, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the illegal Practices of Drovers, Jobbers, and Per Ions, buying and selling again of Live Cattle, tend greatly to enhance the Price of Meat Provisions.

Rfihed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the present Laws li>r reltraining such Practices are insufficient and ineffectual, for want of a more easy Method of convicting Offenders.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Thursday Morning next.

And he further said. That if the Bounty is renewed there would be ioo Ships in a Year or two fitted out from London only, if the Peace continues; and that there will not be a Angle Ship fitted out, if the Bounty is not continued.

That the Sailors employed in this Trade may always be depended on for a certainty, in case of any sudden Kupture in Europe, as the Ships constantly fail the latter End of March or beginning of and return in

Aug'Jt.

That we formerly purchased the Utensils for this Fishery from Foreigners, which are now made at home, and are better than the Dutch can make them, and are a very considerable Branch of Trade at Birmingham and Whitby, and many Manufacturers are employed in making Harpoons, Knives, and Lances, and other Materials; and that the Value of the Fishing Materials amount to about £. 500 upon each Ship.

Mr. James Mather, being examined, said. That the Ships employed in this Trade increased from the Year 1750 (when the 40.s', per Ton Bounty was granted) to 1756 to the Number of 67; and at that Time the War breaking out, they were taken into the Service of the Government as Transports, and the great Advance of Seamens Wages was the reason they did not increase after that Time: That the Expence of fitting out Ships for this Trade is so great, that it is not worth while for Adventurers to engage upon a Bounty which is to continue for Three Years only:

That it has increased in some degree, even though the Bounty was for so thort aTerm, for that the Number of Ships fitted out for this Trade in 1766, was 35 from England and Nine from Scotland; and in 1767 Thirty-five from England and Twelve from Scotland:

That if the Bounty is continued for Seven Years, he believes 150 Sail of Ships will be fitted out fro Britain , that lie has sent Four Ships, and if the Bounty is continued, he will fend Six: That there are 200 Sail of large Ships laid up for want of Employment: That if the Bounty is not continued, the Witness intends to fit out his Ships in Holland, as they may be fitted out at a much cheaper Rate there than in England, as the Duties in Holland upon every Thing used on Board the Greenland Ships are remitted, which is almost equal to our Bounty:

That the Price of Greenland Bone would be, from £. 550 to £. 600 ptrTon, if there were not any Ships sent from this Country; that the Witness fold Four Tons of that Bone lately for 410 per Ton, and t hat the Greenland Bone is of a better Quality than Bone, as it will fell from £. 70 to £. 80 per Ton more:

That if a Ship was to return unsuccessful, though the Owners received the Bounty, they would lose from £. 700 to £. 1,000 a Ship; and if the Bounty was continued for Seven Years longer their would be more Greenland Bone imported; and they should be able to supply the Foreign Market.

Mr. George Campbell, being examined, said. That in the Year 1750, One Ship was fitted out from Liverpool, and in 1756 Two Ships, and since the Peace have increased to Six Ships: That if the Bounty had been renewed from 1764, for Seven Years, he believes, they should have fitted out Twenty Ships: That the Owners are obliged to register the Men, and to take an Apprentice for every Fifty Tons Burthen of the Ship; and that the men used in this Fishery are allowed to be the hardiest of Seamen; and he apprehends that about Twenty new Seamen are made in every Ship upon a Voyage to Greenland: That the Ships always carry more men than they are required by the Act; but that the Officers of the Customs never will muster more than the Act requires: That the Duties paid to the Government for the Materials of a Ship amount to £.150: That the Wages for the Seamen is from $s. to 1 ox. per Month more than in other Trades; V91. 31.

and that if the Bounty is not continued many of the Men employed in this Trade will go into the Dutch Greenland Fill very.

Mr. Samuel Enderby, being examined, said, That he believes, about Six thousand ions of Oil, One thousand of which is imported from Greenland, is annually consumed in this Kingdom: That the First Coll of a Ton of American Oil is about £. 15, and the Charges of bringing it from thence, is about 6 j and if no Oil was to be imported from Greenland he apprehends there would be an Advance of about £. 3 per Ton in the Price.

Mr. Jonathan Delver, a Whalebone Cutter, being examined, said. That the Manufacturers of Whalebone give the Preference to Greenland Bone: That the American Bone is of a large coarse Nature, and is more brittle, and liable to break: That if there is not any Greenland Bone brought here, he should import it from Holland, notwithstanding the re is a Duty of £. 84 per 1'on, and the American Bone is only charged with the old Subsidy, or Twenty-five Shillings per Ton: That all the Bone brought from Greenland is consumed: That 100 Tons of all Sorts of Bone are annually consumed; that the Price of Greenland Bone, is, on an Average, about £. 400 per Ton; and if there is no Bone brought from thence, it may rife £. 100 Ton, and mull be supplied by Foreigners: That there was not any Necessity to import any Greenland Bone from Holland in the Years 1765 and 1766, as the British had a successful Fishefy in Greenland.

Captain Hood informed your Committee, That the Greenland Ships fend more Men than are required by the Act, of which no Account is kept at the Custom House: And that if a Ship returned unsuccessful, though the Bounty was received, there would be a Lose to the Owners of £. 700, or thereabouts.

The Reprimand was as followeth; viz.

Philip Ward, John Treacher, Sir Thomas Munday, Thomas Wife, John Nicholes, John Phillips, Isaac ranee, Richard Taioney, Thomas Robinson, John Browns

THE Offence of which you have been guilty has justly brought you under the severe Displeasure of thisHouse. A more enormous Crime you could not Well T

commit; since a deeper Wound could not be given to the Constitution itself, than by the open and dangerous Attempt which you have made to subvert the Freedom and Independence of this House.

The Freedom of this House in the Freedom of this -Country, which can continue no longer than while the 1

Voices of the Electors are uninfluenced by any base or venal Motive. For if Abilities and Integrity are no Recommendation to the Electors; if those who bid highest for their Voices are to obtain them from such detestable Considerations; this House, will not be the Reprefen-tatives of the people of Great Britain. Instead of being the Guardians and Protestors of their Liberties, instead of redressing the Grievances of the Subject, This House ’

itself will be the Authors of the worst of Grievances:

They will become the venal Instruments of Power to reduce this happy Nation, the Envy and Admiration Of the World, to the lowed State of Misery and Servitude.

This is the abject Condition to which you have attempted to bring your fellow Subjects.

Many Circumstances concur to aggravate your Offence. The Place of your Residence was a Angular Advantage. You had at all Times the example of one of the most learned and respectable Bodies in Europe before your Eyes. Their Conduct in every Instance, but especially in the Choice of their Representativesdn Parliament, was well worthy your Imitation.

You are Magistrates of a Great City. In such a Station, it was a Duty peculiarly incumbent upon you to watch over the Morals of your Fellow Citizens; to keep yourselves pure from Venality; and to prevent, by your Influence, those under your Government from being tainted by this growing and pestilential Vice. It appears, that if the present Application takes Place, the Country Brewing Victualler will not be induced to buy of the Common Brewer, and cease to brew for bim-frl'f, becrause the Course of his Trade would Hill give him Advantages; for though the Brewing Victualler has no Allowance for Leakage, and pays the same Duty as the Country Common Brewer, yet the Country Brewing Victualler brews on the Spot, fells on the Spot, has no Expence of long Carriage, Servants, Horses, Drays, Lois of Calks, Stavage, Leakage, Pillage, and long Credit, fells by retail Measure, and has therefore a greater Profit, which are Advantages which will still induce him to brew for himself; and though the Country Common Brewer may he relieved by this Application, yet the Country Victualling Brewer and the London Common Brewer will not get less.

And it appeared by the Evidence of Mr.

that the Brewers at present keep a larger Stoek than formerly, as nothing but Beer is brewed', That at the time when Ale was brewed, it was a greater Advantage to the Brewer, as his Returns were quicker, and he gave less Credit; and also by the Evidence of Mr. Porter, who added, That the Expence was much in-creaferl in keeping a Stock of Beer, in the Article of Calks; and it also appeared by the Evidence of Mr. Finch, That the greatest Quantity of Strong Beer sold, was in keeping 12 Months and upwards.

And it appeared by the Evidence of Mr. Goodwin, Mr. Porter, and Mr. Finch, that 36 Gallons, as the Law

requires, is always delivered for a Barrel of Beer; and that there is no fncli Measure used in any Malt Liquor as 32 Gallons to the Barrel ever since the Disuse of Ale.

Sir Hugh Dalrymple reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Provost, Magistrates, and Town Council of the Royal Burgh of Dunbar, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had diretf ed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Cleik’s Table: \\ here the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. George Coiveriy being examined, said. That the Town of Dunbar, being situated on a rising Ground, has hitherto been ill supplied with Water; and to remedy which Inconvenience, the Town of Dunbar did enter intoan Agreement with the Proprietor of certain Springs of Water, for supplying the said Town with Water; and that the Proprietors, through whose Grounds the Pipes for conveying the Water were intended to be laid have consented thereto; but as feme of the said Proprietors are only Tenants for Life, and as it has been found necessary to carry the Pipes along one of the County Bridges, and across a Public High Road, and through Part of a Minister’s Glebe, the said Works cannot be completed without the Aid of an Act of Parliament.

Which Evidence was confirmed by a Member present.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better supplying the Town of Dunbar with fresh Water: And that Sir Hugh Dalrymple and Sir Gilbert Elliot do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

of Privilege, hereafter to be made by any Member of this House, if the House shall adjudge that 110 Breach of Privilege has been committed, the Member who made the Complaint shall pay, to the Person complained of, his Costs and Expences incurred by reason of such Complaint;

The Amendments following were proposed to be made to the Question; viz.

Then Mr. Williams, one of the Messengers of the erjeant at Arms attending this House, being called in, informed the House, that he had been at the Lodgings of the said Mr Reynolds, in Scotland Yard; and that he was told by a Servant Maid, that he went out of Town upon Saturday last, and was expected in Town this Day; but that his Return was uncertain.

And then he was again directed to withdraw.

And then he was again directed to be taken from the Bar.

A Petition of Joseph Hickey was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner is now a Prisoner in the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, for having been guilty of a corrupt Attempt to obtain a Seat in this House for a Client by whom he was employed; and that the Petitioner is highly sensible of the Heinousness of his Offence, and unfeignedly sorry for the fame; and representing to the House, that the Continuance of his Confinement will be attended with very ill Consequence to himself and Family; and that the Petitioner has the Conduct of an Opposition to a Bill, now depending in the House of Lords, and committed for Tomorrow, in which he has not been as yet able to instruci his Counsel; and that the Petitioner will he careful fer the future to avoid incurring the Censure of this House: And therefore praying the House to take his same into Consideration, and order him to be discharged.

Ordered, That the said Joseph Hickey be brought to the Bar of this House, Tomorrow Morning, in order to his being discharged.

A Petition of William le March ant, Esquire, Agent for the Island of Guernsey, was presented to the House, and read; Stating the Hardships which, the Petitioner alleges, the Inhabitants, and the Trade and Navigation of that Bland labour under, in consequence of a Clause in an Act passed in the Fourth Year of His prefect Majesty, by which it is enacted, That neither the Allowance of £. 12 per Cent, theretofore granted, nor any other Allowance, for Leakage upon Wines imported into this Kingdom, lliould be made, unless such Wines be imported directly from the Country or Place of the Growth of the said Wine, or the usual Port or Place of its first Shipping, except only Madeira Wines, imported from any of the British Colonies or Plantations in America, or from the East Indies; and reprefeming to the House, that, although the said Clause has, in its Consequences, proved so very prejudicial to the said Bland of Guernsey, yet, it is not likely to be of any Benefit to the Revenue of this Kingdom, as will appear from a Report of the Commissioners of His Majesty’s Customs, made to the Lords Commissioners of FI is Majesty’s Treasury, on the 27th March 1766, v.herein they give their Opinion, " That the said Clause with respect to the " Blands of Guernsey and Jerj'ey ought to be repealed: " And therefore praying. That a Clause may be inserted in some Bill, for allowing the said £. 12 per Cent, for Leakage on Wines brought into this Kingdom, from the Blands of Guernsey and Jerj'ey, in like Manner as the same had been used to be allowed before the passing of the said Act of the Fourth Y'ear of the Reign of His present Majesty.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Confuleration of a Committee of the whole House.

A Petition of the principal Land Owners, and Proprietors of Estates, in the Parish of Christ Church, in the County of Surrey, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is depending, for making One or more Road or Roads, from the South End of the Bridge cross the River Thames, from Black Friars, in the City of London, to the opposite Shore, in the County of Surrey; and for making, widening, and improving, several Communications between the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Town and Borough of Southwark, and for other Purposes; and that several of the Provisions and Claufps in the said Bill will, if passed into a Law, be extremely prejudicial to the Estates and Interei s of the Petitioners: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill, as may affect them; and that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for making One or more Road or Roads, from the South End of the Bridge cross the River Thames, from Black Friars, in the City of London, to the opposite Shore, in the County of Surrey, and for making, widening, and improving, several Communications, between the Cities of Londim and Westminster, and the Town and Borough of Southwark; and for impowering the Trustees for carrying into Execution an Act, passed in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, to make, open, and keep in Repair, and also to watch and light, certain Roads, necessary to open the Communication between Christ Church, near the said Bridge, and the Counties of Surrey, Kent, Suffer, and Southampton’, and to keep in Repair, watch, and light, a new Road, from Christ Church, to Westminster Bridge; be read a Second Time.

Buckland Brewer to £.231; Northam to £. 321; and Ware Giffard to £.90. 6 s.; at which Rate, or in Proportion thereto, the said respective Parishes have, for more than Sixty Years, been aftefted, and by this Means, as the Petitioners have found, there hath also been an annual Deficiency in the Sum upon the whole Division; and that by an Act, made in 1747, all Arrears of Land Tax were generally remitted, and forgiven to that Time; and that the said Mode of Assessment having subsisted for near Sixty Years, without Objection, the Petitioners were greatly surprised, when they were given to understand, that there was a considerable Arrear of Tax due from the said Division; and that, being returned insuper thereon into the Court of Exchequer, in or about Trinity Term, 1764, Process had issued for the fame, out of the said Court, and therein the said Arrears are charged to the said Division, or Hundred, at large, correspondingwiththesaidoriginalAfleftinent in 1693; and that the Petitioners are willing to make good, in future, the Quota originally aftefted on the said Division; but the raising the said Arrears will be attended with great Hardship to such of the Petitioners on whom such Burthen shall fall, in regard that the Petitioners have already regularly discharged the several Payments with which they have been respectively aftefted, and which have been as high or higher, than most of their Neighbours, in that Part of the Kingdom, the said Town of Bideford in particular, and the said other Parishes at present have very few Inhabitants capable of bearing any Charge, in respect of their Personal Estate; and much the greatest Part of the Petitioners, as well those whose Lands lie within the said Town, as those within the said Division at large, have become Purchasers, for a valuable Consideration, of their respective Properties, within the said Division and Town, without the least Knowledge, or Notice, that the same were liable to such Arrears of Land Tax: And therefore praying the House to take the said same into consideration, and to grant unto the Petitioners such Relief therein, as the Nature of the same requires, and as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Lecturers of Grefliam College, was presented to the Heuse, and read; Taking Notice of the said Bill; and setting forth, That, by the Will of Sir Thomas Grefliam, Knight, Founder of the said College, it was directed, that the Seven Persons elected and appointed to read the Lectures in the said Will mentioned, should have the Occupation of his Mansion House, Gardens, and other Appurtenances (now called Gresham CollegeJy for them and every of them, there to inhabit, study, and daily to read the said several Lectures; and that, in and by the said Will, it is further directed, that none should be chosen to read any of the said Lectures so long as he should be married, nor be suffered to read any of the said Lectures after he should be married; neither should receive any Fee, or Stipend, appointed for the reading of the said Lectures; and that, as the said College will be pulled down in pursuance of the Bill now depending, and that Part of the Will of the said Sir Thomas Grefliam by which the Occupation of the said College is given to the said Lefturers, made null and void: Therefore praying the House, That as the Collegiate Life, intended by Sir Thomas Gresham, will now ueceflarily be at an End, the Restriction contained in the said Will, with respect to the Marriage of the said Lecturers, may also be taken away; and that Provision may be made for that Purpose, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Conv-mittee, that they have Power to receive a Clause, or Clauses, to enable the Lecturers of the College, called Gresham College, founded by Sir Thomas Gresham, Knight, to marry, notwithstanding any Restriction contained in the Will of the said Sir Thomas Gresham.

Resolved, That it is the opinion of this Committee,

That Grey or Scrow Salt, Salt Scale, Sand Scaje, Cruii-ings, or other Foul Salt, be. allowed to be taken from the Salt Works in England, Wales, or Berwick upon Tiveed, to be used as Manure, upon Payment of a Duty of Four Pence per Bushel only.

Resolved, That it is the opinion of this Committee,

That all Policies, by which the Property of One Person, or of a particular Number of Persons in one general Partnership, or of One Body Politic or Corporate, in any Ship or Cargo, or both, shall be allured, to the Amount of more than One thousand Pounds, be stamped with Two Five Shillings Stamps.

Resolved, That it is the opinion of this Committee,

That so much of an Act, made in the Thirty-third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act for encouraging the Exportation of Rum, and Spirits of the Growth, Produce, and Manufacture of the British Sugar Plantations, from this Kingdom, and of British Spirits, made from Molasses, as directs that the Rum, or Spirits, of the Growth, Produce, and Manufactures of the British Sugar Plantations in America, which should be intitled to the Allowance of the Duty of Custom, and freed from the Duty of Excise, on Exportation thereof, should be Proof Spirits, be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That upon the Exportation of such Rum, or Spirits, there be an Allowance, or Drawback, of all the Duties of Customs payable upon the importation thereof; and that such Rum, or Spirits, be freed and discharged from all the Duties of Excise, though the same iliaii not be }

Proof Spirits.

The King*! After which His Majesty was pleased to make a most Speech. gracious Speech from the Throne, to both 1 loufes of Parliament, as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The Readiness with which you entered into the Views I recommended to you at the Opening of this Session, and the Assiduity with which you have applied yourselves to the Dispatch of the Public Buii-ness, give Me great Satisfaction. At the same Time, the affectionate Concern you have lliewn for the Welfare of your Fellow Subjects, by the salutary Laws passed for their Relief, in respect to the high Price of Provisions, cannot fail of securing to you their most grateful Regard.

I have nothing new to communicate to you in relation to Foreign Affairs. The apparent Interests of the several Powers in Europe, as well as the express Assurances I have received from them, leave Me no room

to doubt of their Disposition to preserve the general Tranquillity. And, on My Part, you may rest allured, that every Meafiire that is confident with the Honour of My Crown, and the Rights of M v Subjects, shall be Readily directed to that moll salutary Purpol'e.

Gentlemen of the Floufe of Commons,

Yuor Cheerfulness in granting the necessary Supplies, and your Attent ion to the lvafe of My good Subjects in the Manner of railing them, equally demand My Acknowledgments: I lee, with Pleasure, that you have been able to prosecute your Plan for the Diminution of the National Debt, without laying any additional Burthen upon My People.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

As the Time limited by Law for the Expiration of th is Parliament now draws near, I have refoived forthwith to issue My Proclamation for ditVolvinit, and so: calling a new Parliament. But I cannot do this, without having iirlt returned you My Thanks for the many signal Proofs you have given of the mo ft affectionate Attachment to My Person, Family, and Government, the most faithful Attention to the Public Service, and the most earnclt Zeal for the Preservation of our excellent Cunftitution. When, by the vigorous Support which you gave Meduring the War, 1 had been tumbled, under the Divine Providence, to rest ore to My IVoph-the Biellings of Peace, you continued to exert yourselves, with equal Alacrity and Sb adiness, in purluing every Measure that could contribute to tla* Ntainrenaujc of the Public Safety and Tranquillity; which you well 1 understood could no otherwise be preferred than b y efa-blishing, on a respeetable Foundation, the Strength, the Credit, and the Commerce of the Nation. The large Supplies you have from Time to Time granted, and the wife Regulations you have made for these important Purposes, will, I am persuaded, be found to have been productive of the moll beneficial Consequences.

In the approaching Election of Representatives, I doubt not but My People will give Mofrefh Proofs of their Attachment to the true Interest of their Country; which I shall ever receive as the mart; acceptable Mark of their inflection Me. The Welfare of all My Subjects is My first Object. Nothing the refore has ever given Me more real Concern than to Ice any of them, many Part of My Dominions,attemptingtoloofen those Bonds of Confiitutional Subordination so eftential to the Welfare of the Whoje. But it is with much Satisfaction that I now fee them returning to a more jntl Sense of what their own Interest, no less them their Duty, indispensably requires of them; and thereby giving Me the Prolpect of continuing to reign over an happy, because an united People,

After which the Lord Chancellor, by His Majesty’s Command, said;

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is His Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure, that this pjflh* Parliament be prorogued to this Day Three Weeks, the Thirty-first Day of this nstant March; and this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to this Day ihree Weeks, the Thirty-lirst Day of this Inliant March.
